column4: Preferences of a Voice-First Nation: Large-Scale Pairwise Evaluation and Preference Analysis for TTS in Indian Languages
column6: Crowdsourced pairwise evaluation has emerged as a scalable approach for assessing foundation models. However, applying it to Text to Speech(TTS) introduces high variance due to linguistic diversity and multidimensional nature of speech perception. We present a controlled multidimensional pairwise evaluation framework for multilingual TTS that combines linguistic control with perceptually grounded annotation. Using 5K+ native and code-mixed sentences across 10 Indic languages, we evaluate 7 state-of-the-art TTS systems and collect over 120K pairwise comparisons from over 1900 native raters. In addition to overall preference, raters provide judgments across 6 perceptual dimensions: intelligibility, expressiveness, voice quality, liveliness, noise, and hallucinations. Using Bradley-Terry modeling, we construct a multilingual leaderboard, interpret human preference using SHAP analysis and analyze leaderboard reliability alongside model strengths and trade-offs across perceptual dimensions.
column7: Srija Anand(IIT Madras; AI4Bharat); Ashwin Sankar(IIT Madras; AI4Bharat); Ishvinder Sethi(AI4Bharat); Aaditya Pareek(Josh Talks); Kartik Rajput(AI4Bharat); Gaurav Yadav(Josh Talks); Nikhil Narasimhan(AI4Bharat); Adish Pandya(IIT Madras); Deepon Halder(IIT Madras); Mohammed Safi Ur Rahman Khan(IIT Madras; AI4Bharat); Praveen S V(IIT Madras; AI4Bharat); Shobhit Banga(Josh Talks); Mitesh M Khapra(IIT Madras; AI4Bharat)

column4: Application context in speech synthesis evaluation: A problem and a solution
column6: Advancements in research of synthetic speech can only be properly quantified and driven by well-proven evaluation procedures, the most prevalent of which being the subjective listening test. In this paper, the ecological validity of such tests is evaluated empirically in an experiment comparing rating outcomes of four synthetic speech systems across four different application contexts. It is shown that, depending on the scenario in which they are obtained, the ratings for a respective synthesis system change significantly. Additionally, it is found that the impact of the application also depends on the system in question, highlighting a potential confound in evaluations comparing systems without a specified application context. Further, it is discovered that ratings collected in a digital twin provide statistically equivalent ratings to the ones obtained in a physical setting, suggesting that simulation testing might prove a beneficial path to achieving ecologically valid evaluations.
column7: Fritz Seebauer(Bielefeld University); Markus Rothgänger(Bielefeld University); Sven Wachsmuth(Bielefeld University); Petra Wagner(Bielefeld University)

column4: Is Natural Always Appropriate? Investigating Naturalness and Appropriateness Across Different Domains for TTS Evaluation
column6: Text-to-speech (TTS) evaluation is an open challenge. While the primary target was "naturalness," recent fidelity gains shifted focus toward "appropriateness" and whether speech is correct for its context. In this work, we examine how perception changes when the expected downstream use varies. We measure the appropriateness and human-likeness of five SOTA TTS systems across five domains: AI assistant, reader, actor, animated character, and spontaneous speaker. Results show appropriateness varies across domains independently of naturalness. While systems shine at reading, expressive domains remain challenging, and optimizing for one can degrade others. Furthermore, naturalness scores tend to penalize stylized speech while rewarding spontaneity. Finally, our study also highlights blind spots in one-size-fits-all evaluation metrics across more expressive domains. We demonstrate that TTS performance is not "solved" but depends on the target domain, requiring context-aware evaluation.
column7: Dominika Woszczyk(Iconic); Andreas Triantafyllopoulos(TUM); Jura Miniota(KTH); Éva Székely(KTH); Bjoern Schuller(TUM; Imperial College London)

column4: NV-Bench: Benchmark of Nonverbal Vocalization Synthesis for Expressive Text-to-Speech Generation
column6: While recent text-to-speech (TTS) systems increasingly integrate nonverbal vocalizations (NVs), their evaluations lack standardized metrics and reliable ground-truth references. To bridge this gap, we propose NV-Bench, the first benchmark grounded in a functional taxonomy that treats NVs as communicative acts rather than acoustic artifacts. NV-Bench comprises 1,651 multi-lingual, in-the-wild utterances with paired human reference audio, balanced across 14 NV categories. We introduce a dual-dimensional evaluation protocol: (1) Instruction Alignment, utilizing the proposed paralinguistic character error rate (PCER) to assess controllability, (2) Acoustic Fidelity, measuring the distributional gap to real recordings to assess acoustic realism. We evaluate diverse TTS models and develop two baselines. Experimental results demonstrate a strong correlation between our objective metrics and human perception, establishing NV-Bench as a standardized evaluation framework.
column7: Qinke Ni(The Chinese University of Hong Kong-Shenzhen); Huan Liao(The Chinese University of Hong Kong-Shenzhen); Dekun Chen(The Chinese University of Hong Kong-Shenzhen); Yuxiang Wang(The Chinese University of Hong Kong-Shenzhen); Zhizheng Wu(The Chinese University of Hong Kong-Shenzhen; Shenzhen Loop Area Institute; Amphion Technology Co.,Ltd)

column4: Phonetically Grounded Vowel Space Metrics for Evaluating Synthetic Speech During TTS Model Training
column6: Synthetic speech is generally evaluated using subjective listening tests, which are costly and impractical to perform during text-to-speech (TTS) model training. Traditional loss curves in model training lack linguistic interpretability and fail to reflect perceptual changes. We propose using phonetically grounded objective metrics, Vowel Space Overlap and Procrustes Normalised Disparity, to evaluate synthetic speech during training by quantifying the similarity between synthesised and ground-truth vowel space shapes. We fine-tuned a TTS model on two accents, computed the metrics at training steps, and conducted perception tests to assess the relationship between the metrics and perceived accent similarity. Our results show significant correlations between metrics and accent perception across both accents. This suggests that the proposed metrics provide reliable, perceptually meaningful, and interpretable complements to loss curves for evaluating synthetic speech during training.
column7: Pasindu Udawatta(University of Auckland); Jesin James(University of Auckland); Ake Nicholas(University of Auckland); B. T. Balamurali(Independent Researcher); C. I. Watson(University of Auckland)

column4: The Binding Effect: Analysis of How Multi-Dimensional Cues Form Gender Bias in Instruction TTS
column6: Current bias evaluations in Instruction Text-to-Speech (ITTS) often rely on univariate testing, overlooking the compositional structure of social cues. In this work, we investigate gender bias by modeling prompts as combinations of Social Status, Career stereotypes, and Persona descriptors. Analyzing open-source ITTS models, we uncover systematic interaction effects where social dimensions modulate one another, creating complex bias patterns missed by univariate baselines. Crucially, our findings indicate that these biases extend beyond surface-level artifacts, demonstrating strong associations with the semantic priors of pre-trained text encoders and the skewed distributions inherent in training data. We further demonstrate that generic diversity prompting is insufficient to override these entrenched patterns, underscoring the need for compositional analysis to diagnose latent risks in generative speech.
column7: Kuan-Yu Chen(National Taiwan University; Inventec Corporation); Yi-Cheng Lin(National Taiwan University); Po-Chung Hsieh(National Taiwan University); Huang-Cheng Chou(University of Southern California); Chih-Fan Hsu(Inventec Corporation); Jeng-Lin Li(Inventec Corporation); Hung-yi Lee(National Taiwan University); Jian-Jiun Ding(National Taiwan University)

column1: Tuesday 29 September 2026 - 14:00-16:00 - Area 8 - Oral 1 - Audio Language Models

column4: Recent advances in speech language model for ASR
column6: With recent advances in large language models (LLMs), both academia and industry have increasingly focused on developing speech LLMs by integrating the speech modality into LLM architectures. This talk centers on recent progress in speech-LLM for automatic speech recognition (ASR). While standard speech-LLM approaches have reached maturity, as evidenced by state-of-the-art results on major leaderboards, I will delve into topics such as unleashing the full potential of LLMs, long-form speech modeling, and decoding acceleration. I will also introduce recent breakthroughs in encoder-free speech-LLMs, which pave the way toward truly native multimodal language models that process speech as naturally as text.

column4: HybridCodec: Modeling Discrete and Continuous Representations For Efficient Speech Language Models
column6: Discrete audio representations have become increasingly popular for building multimodal text-audio systems and integrating audio capabilities into Large Language Models (LLMs). However, numerous studies report performance degradation on various downstream tasks due to information loss during discretization. To address this, we propose a novel approach combining temporally compressed discrete tokens with dimensionality-reduced continuous residuals. Our framework consists of a hybridized discrete-continuous focal modulation codec and a hybrid Transformer. This architecture performs autoregressive inference in the discrete domain, coupled with non-autoregressive prediction and continuous residual upsampling. Experimental results show that our approach significantly improves the retention of speaker characteristics compared to discrete-only methods, while simultaneously reducing the number of required autoregressive steps.
column7: Artem Ploujnikov(Mila Quebec AI Institute; Concordia University); Francesco Verdini(Sapienza University of Rome); Samir Sadok(Inria, Université Grenoble Alpes CNRS); Mirco Ravanelli(Mila Quebec AI Institute; Concordia University)

column4: TASTE-Streaming: Towards Streamable Text-Aligned Speech Tokenization and Embedding for Spoken Language Modeling
column6: Text-speech joint spoken language modeling (SLM) aims at natural and intelligent speech-based interactions, but developing such a system may suffer from modality mismatch: speech unit sequences are much longer than text tokens. Prior work reduces this gap with text-aligned tokenization and embedding (TASTE), producing speech tokens that align in lengths with their textual counterparts. However, the dependence on an external ASR system and the use of a non-causal decoder limits streaming use. To address this limitation, we propose TASTE-S, a streamable extension of TASTE suitable for real-time usage. TASTE-S integrates a CTC-based ASR module into the encoder for instant dual-modality encoding. We also redesign the unit decoder to enable on-the-fly decoding. With joint training, we show that TASTE-S matches TASTE's performance while significantly reducing latency. Further investigations reveal that TASTE-S remains robust to transcriptions and enables long-form encoding and decoding.
column7: Liang-Hsuan Tseng(National Taiwan University); Hung-yi Lee(National Taiwan University)

column4: Investigating Faithfulness in Large Audio Language Models
column6: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) integrate audio encoders with pretrained Large Language Models to perform complex multimodal reasoning tasks. While these models can generate Chain-of-Thought (CoT) explanations, the faithfulness of these reasoning chains remains unclear. In this work, we propose a systematic framework to evaluate CoT faithfulness in LALMs with respect to both the input audio and the final model prediction. We define three criteria for audio faithfulness: hallucination-free, holistic, and attentive listening. We also introduce a benchmark based on both audio and CoT interventions to assess faithfulness¹. Experiments on Audio Flamingo 3 and Qwen2.5-Omni suggest a potential multimodal disconnect: reasoning often aligns with the final prediction but is not always strongly grounded in the audio and can be vulnerable to hallucinations or adversarial perturbations.
column7: Pooneh Mousavi(Concordia University; Mila - Quebec AI Institute); Lovenya Jain(Birla Institute of Technology and Science); Mirco Ravanelli(Concordia University; Mila - Quebec AI Institute); Cem Subakan(Université Laval; Mila - Quebec AI Institute)

column4: IndicContextEval: A Benchmark for Evaluating Context Utilisation in Audio Large Language Models Across 8 Indic Languages
column6: AudioLLMs enable speech recognition conditioned on textual prompts such as domain descriptions or entity lists. However, it remains unclear whether these models genuinely utilise such context or rely on parametric knowledge learned during pretraining. Existing benchmarks cannot answer this question because they evaluate transcription under fixed prompting conditions and rarely include explicit contextual inputs. We introduce IndicContextEval, a 56-hour multilingual benchmark of natural speech from 555 speakers across 8 Indian languages and 23 professional domains. We design a 7-level prompting framework that progressively introduces contextual signals, including metadata, natural-language descriptions, entity lists in English and native script, and adversarial prompts with incorrect entities. Evaluating five models reveals substantial differences in context utilisation behaviour, highlighting the need for explicit evaluation of contextual grounding in AudioLLMs.
column7: Sakshi Joshi(IIT Madras); Dhruv Subhash Rathi(Sarvam AI); Sanskar Singh(Sarvam AI); Eldho Ittan George(AI4Bharat); R J Hari(IIT Madras); Kaushal Bhogale(IIT Madras); Mitesh M. Khapra(IIT Madras)

column1: Tuesday 29 September 2026 - 14:00-16:00 - Area 13 - Oral 8 - Clinically Useful Speech Representations 2

column4: Clinically meaningful speech representations
column6: While modern speech models can learn powerful representations that achieve impressive predictive performance, high accuracy alone has not translated into widespread clinical adoption. Bridging this gap requires representations that are interpretable, robust across populations, tasks, languages, and recording conditions, sensitive to clinically meaningful change, reliable across participants longitudinally, validated against relevant clinical constructs and outcomes, and ultimately, used to support decisions in real-world studies. This talk surveys the evolution of clinically meaningful speech representations, illustrating key developments with examples from research across ALS, Parkinson’s disease, schizophrenia, depression, autism, and cognitive impairment. We will examine approaches and challenges to combining the power of state-of-the-art models, composite measures and scalable multimodal assessment on the one hand with interpretability, psychometric rigor, and clinical validation on the other in order to transform speech representations from merely being compelling lab research into becoming useful real-world clinical tools.

column4: Reducing Measurement Noise in Digital Speech Biomarkers: Interpretable Composite Index Scores for Longitudinal ALS Monitoring in Clinical Trials
column6: Digital speech measures are promising for remote monitoring of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). However, single speech features can be sensitive to measurement noise. In this work, composite index scores, with feature weights estimated from a natural history dataset, were evaluated for reliability, measurement error, and their ability to capture disease progression on the VRG50635 ALS clinical trial data. We conducted a systematic psychometric evaluation to quantify measurement error reduction in composite scores relative to their constituent features. Linear mixed effects models were applied to assess longitudinal change relative to the ALSFRS-R. The results show that index scores have excellent ICC (> 0.9) and reduce the MDC compared to individual features, while maintaining sensitivity to track longitudinal changes. Our findings show that composite index scores can be applied across datasets and provide great potential as robust endpoints in clinical trials.
column7: Michael Neumann(Modality.AI); Hardik Kothare(Modality.AI); Diego Cadavid(Verge Genomics); Robert H. Scannevin(Verge Genomics); Anil Tarachandani(Verge Genomics); Ines Hoffmann(Verge Genomics); Tara Haley(Verge Genomics); Shane Raines(2b Analytics); Vikram Ramanarayanan(Modality.AI; University of California)

column4: Task-Conditioned Audio-Text-Image Fusion for Cognitive Score Estimation from Speech-Based Assessments
column6: People with mild cognitive impariment tend to perform speech-based tasks differently than the healthy population. In picture description tasks, they often describe a narrower portion of the scene, missing details and spatial relations. We propose a multimodal framework for estimating cognitive assessment scores (MoCA and MMSE) from speech-based cognitive tasks. The model uses pretrained encoders for audio, text, and optional vision, followed by modality-specific projections and task-conditioned fusion. We compare staged variants from acoustic features to foundation-model embeddings, late fusion, mid-level cross-attention fusion, and a final mixture-of-experts model. We also introduce a label-conditioned image-text alignment loss for picture description samples to model differences in transcript-image consistency between healthy controls and patients with mild cognitive impairment. The best model achieved 2.11(+-0.03) MoCA RMSE and 1.85(+-0.08) MMSE RMSE in picture description task.
column7: Justyna Krzywdziak(AGH University of Krakow; Samsung R&D Institute); Władysław Średniawa(Samsung R&D Institute); Agnieszka Pruszek(Samsung R&D Institute); Wojciech Szecówka(AGH University of Krakow; Samsung R&D Institute); Michał Grzeszczyk(Samsung R&D Institute); Teresa Brzozka(Samsung R&D Institute); Bartłomiej Eljasiak(Samsung R&D Institute); Zofia Marciniak(Samsung R&D Institute); Łukasz Lazarski(Samsung R&D Institute); Mateusz Matuszewski(Samsung R&D Institute); Daria Hemmerling(AGH University of Krakow; Samsung R&D Institute)

column4: Analyzing Longitudinal Vocal Changes During Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Hikikomori Patients
column6: Monitoring treatment response during Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) is challenging due to the lack of objective, temporally grounded markers. This study investigates longitudinal vocal dynamics in hikikomori patients undergoing CBT using session-level speech recordings. First, stable Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs) that exhibited consistent temporal variation and low early inter-subject variability were identified. Trajectory analyses then revealed distinct speech evolution patterns between patients showing clinical improvement or deterioration. Finally, Wav2vec 2.0 embeddings were compared with traditional acoustic features. The fusion of Wav2vec 2.0 with MFCCs and fundamental frequency (F0) achieved the highest F1-score across age and gender groups, indicating the complementary value of deep and hand-crafted descriptors. Overall, treatment outcomes were captured more accurately by trajectory evolution than by static pre-post differences.
column7: Samara S. Leal(University of Milan); Stavros Ntalampiras(University of Milan); Antonio Trabacca(Scientific Institute IRCCS “E. Medea”, Scientific Direction); Marcella Bellani(University of Verona; AOUI); Roberto Sassi(University of Milan)

column4: Acoustic Biomarkers of Sleep Deprivation on French Read Speech: Interpretable and Frugal Modeling of Sleep Deprivation and Its Symptoms
column6: Sleep deprivation and its consequences are a major public and personal health issue. In this study, we draw on the SOMVOICE corpus to estimate sleep deprivation and its symptoms (sleepiness, fatigue, performance loss) using speech samples. We prioritised interpretability and frugality, using simple yet robust and validated acoustic features (eGeMAPS and Snack) and classifiers (SVM, Random Forest, Gradient Boost). We evaluated the sex-and age-related biases of our classifier, and reported our energy consumption and carbon footprint. Using SHAP values, we investigated the relative importance of each feature to the classification, allowing comparison with previous studies and driving the field towards mechanistic approaches. Finally, using a symptom network and performing cross-task evaluation, we investigated whether the classifiers had generalised the task they had been trained on, or a more general, less specific construct.
column7: Vincent P. Martin(INRIA Nancy, LORIA; UMons); Jean-Luc Rouas(LaBRI; CNRS); Pierre Philip(SANPSY; CHU de Bordeaux)

column1: ★ Tuesday 29 September 2026 - 14:00-16:00 - Long Oral 6 - Audio Coding and Signal Analysis [Cross-area long papers Oral session]

column4: Representational Instability in Decoupled Audio Encoders
column6: Modern audio processing uses neural encoders to generate discrete or continuous representations for downstream models (e.g., LLMs, ASR). While optimized for the Rate-Distortion (RD) trade-off to ensure waveform reconstruction, their stability is often overlooked. We conceptualize the Stability-Rate-Distortion (SRD) trade-off, highlighting representational stability as a third evaluation axis. Optimizing strictly for reconstruction leaves representations vulnerable to acoustic nuisances, creating a Stability Penalty. To evaluate this, we introduce the Continuous Edit Distance (CED) to quantify geometric drift. Analyzing state-of-the-art encoders (EnCodec, SoundStream, Whisper) reveals catastrophic instability. While continuous latents resist minor perturbations, the vector quantization (VQ) bottleneck shatters them into disparate discrete sequences—the Quantization Penalty. Evaluating 26 dialects exposes a cross-lingual "Language Tax," where stability collapses on low-resource dialects due to weak linguistic priors. High waveform fidelity is empirically at odds with representational stability in low-bitrate regimes, highlighting a critical vulnerability in current audio tokens.
column7: Ehsan Variani(Google Research); Tom Bagby(Google Research); Georg Heigold(Google Research); Ke Wu(Google Research); Cyril Allauzen(Google Research)

column4: DTM-Codec: Dynamic Token Masking for VFR Speech Coding with Efficient Boundary Selection
column6: Variable frame rate (VFR) coding has recently emerged in neural speech codecs, allocating fewer frames to redundant regions and more frames to rapidly changing speech. VFR must transmit side information about retained time steps, but prior gains are either not rigorously addressed or often minor once these overhead bits are included in total bitrate. We present Dynamic Token Masking (DTM)-Codec, a neural speech codec that demonstrates clear gains over fixed-frame-rate baselines under a strict matched-total-bitrate protocol. DTM keeps selected encoder tokens, fills masked positions with a learned <MASK> embedding, and transmits a binary keep-mask for position-aware decoding. We further introduce Path Length Equalization (PLE), a linear-time boundary selector for VFR coding that yields well-spread adaptive segments with negligible overhead. Across operating points, DTM-Codec broadly improves reconstruction quality and intelligibility over fixed-frame-rate baselines.
column7: Hoyeol Sohn(KAIST); Juhan Nam(KAIST)

column4: HARP: Harmonic-Aware Residual Partitioning for Neural Audio Codecs
column6: Neural audio codecs with residual vector quantization (RVQ) normally treat all frequencies uniformly, so their codebooks become spectrally entangled. Truncating stages then removes an unpredictable mix of frequencies. Parallel band decomposition addresses this by splitting audio into independent bands, but fragments the latent space and loses cross-frequency coherence. We introduce HARP (Harmonic-Aware Residual Partitioning), a training strategy that partitions RVQ stages into frequency-ordered groups where each group refines its target band while the decoder retains access to all lower frequencies. Overtones are reconstructed in the context of their fundamentals, preserving coherence that parallel methods lose. HARP requires no architectural changes; it only modifies the training loss, leaving inference identical to standard RVQ. On speech, music, and general audio, HARP outperforms both standard RVQ and parallel decomposition. MUSHRA listening tests also show perceptual improvements.
column7: Qiaoyu Yang(Georgia Institute of Technology); Lixing He(The Chinese University of Hong Kong; Tencent Music Entertainment); Binyue Deng(Georgia Institute of Technology); Weifeng Zhao(Tencent Music Entertainment)

column4: Sleep Sound Event Detection Powered by Learnable Multi-Resolution Adaptive Line Enhancer
column6: Sleep-disordered breathing, including snoring, hypopnea, and obstructive apnea, is the hallmark of obstructive sleep apnea, whose severity is quantified by the Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI). As conventional polysomnography is costly and clinically demanding, microphone-only detection has emerged as a noninvasive alternative for screening. We propose ALE-Confidence Fusion Sound Event Detection (ACF-SED), the first framework that directly injects the per-frame confidence map of an Adaptive Line Enhancer (ALE) into Transformer attention biasing and feature modulation, rather than as mere preprocessing. A Multi-Resolution ALE Bank aggregates three parallel NLMS filters at distinct decorrelation delays, while a Confidence-Guided Cross-Path block couples event and noise streams via gated cross-attention. On the Audio-Polygraphy Dataset for Sleep Apnea Analysis, ACF-SED achieves state-of-the-art detection across Event-F1, Segment-F1, and PSDS, enabling end-to-end AHI estimation.
column7: Chanwoo Park(Korea University); Chanwoo Kim(Korea University)

column4: Similarity as Evidence: An Explainable Siamese Framework for Snore Sound Classification
column6: Snore sounds are clinically informative acoustic biomarkers, yet robust and transparent automatic classification remains challenging. We propose an explainable Siamese framework for four-class snore classification that treats similarity as decision evidence. A lightweight convolution module learns ℓ₂-normalised embeddings using joint semi-hard triplet and class-balanced cross-entropy training. Classification is performed via a non-parametric Class Centroid aligned with metric learning. A support-based explanation mechanism relates predictions to reference examples and visually comparable time-frequency activation patterns. On the Munich-Passau Snore Sound Corpus, macro-recall improves from 0.401 (wav2vec2) to 0.638 and remains robust under additive noise. Deletion and perturbation tests validate explanation faithfulness and stability, demonstrating interpretable similarity-based reasoning for clinical sleep assessment.
column7: Boyang Meng(Beijing Institute of Technology); Mengkai Sun(Beijing Institute of Technology); Haojie Zhang(Beijing Institute of Technology); Kun Qian(Beijing Institute of Technology); Wei Xue(Hong Kong University of Science and Technology); Bin Hu(Beijing Institute of Technology); Björn W. Schuller(TUM University Hospital)

column4: Beyond Deep Learning: Speech Segmentation and Phone Classification with Neural Assemblies
column6: Deep learning dominates speech processing but relies on massive datasets, backpropagation, and produces dense representations. Assembly Calculus (AC), which models sparse neuronal assemblies with Hebbian plasticity and winner-take-all competition, offers a biologically grounded alternative. We introduce an AC-based speech processing framework that operates directly on continuous speech by combining three key contributions: (i) neural encoding that converts speech into assembly-compatible spike patterns; (ii) a multi-area architecture organising assemblies across hierarchical timescales and classes; and (iii) cross-area update schemes. Applied to two tasks of boundary detection and segment classification, our framework detects phone (F1=0.69) and word (F1=0.61) boundaries without weight training and achieves 47.5% and 45.1% accuracy on phone and command recognition. These results show that AC-based dynamical systems are a promising alternative to deep learning for speech.
column7: Trevor Adelson(The University of Melbourne); Vidhyasaharan Sethu(University of New South Wales); Ting Dang(The University of Melbourne)

column1: Tuesday 29 September 2026 - 14:00-16:00 - Area 2 - Poster 4 - Perception and Appraisal of Prosody

column4: Positioning Effect of Syllable Shortening on Speech Segmentation: Evidence from Mandarin Listeners
column6: This study examines how syllable shortening influences speech segmentation using an artificial language experiment. While listeners use transitional probabilities and salient prosodic cues, reduced prosody such as syllable shortening remains understudied. Native Mandarin listeners (N = 120) learned trisyllabic artificial words under conditions shortening either the initial, middle, or final syllable. Results showed that middle-syllable shortening facilitated segmentation, final-syllable shortening hindered it, and initial shortening had no clear effect. The findings indicate that durational reduction aids segmentation when aligned with predictable word internal structure but disrupts it when applied at word boundaries.
column7: Shu-Chen Ou(National Sun Yat-sen University)

column4: Perceptual Trade-offs Across Segmental and Suprasegmental Levels: Comparing Ganong Patterns in Mandarin Consonants and Lexical Tones
column6: The Ganong effect shows how lexical knowledge biases the perception of ambiguous speech, yet whether this mechanism generalizes across segmental and suprasegmental levels remains unclear. Using a within-subject design (N = 57), we compared acoustic-phonetic processing (identification slopes) and lexical reliance (Ganong effect) for Mandarin tones and consonants. Across levels, neither measure was reliably correlated within individuals, indicating that both capacities are largely level-specific. Yet the underlying weighting mechanism was shared: at both levels, individuals with less precise acoustic-phonetic processing showed a larger Ganong effect. These findings support a reliability-based weighting principle: although the processing resources devoted to specific cues vary across levels, individuals apply a common strategy, weighting lexical knowledge against acoustic-phonetic reliability to resolve ambiguity.
column7: Jiaxin LI(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Yi Weng(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Yicheng Rong(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Gang Peng(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University)

column4: Rhythmic Patterning in Vietnamese: The Case of Quadrisyllabic Reduplicative Words
column6: The Vietnamese prosody literature identifies conflicting views on the existence of stress, the pattern of a stress unit, and its prosodic status. This lack of consensus motivated further investigation into rhythmic patterning in Vietnamese. Eight native speakers read a list of eight existing morphosyntactically head-initial and head-final quadrisyllabic reduplicative words, framed in three carrier sentences varying in the number of syllables before and after the target word. An iambic pattern was observed in syllable duration rather than mean rhyme F0 and intensity ratio. The second and fourth syllables were significantly longer than the first and third, respectively. Different carrier sentences did not change the overall rhythmic pattern. These findings support the presence of word-level stress and iambic rhythm, suggesting the possibility of a foot domain in Vietnamese. However, they do not support the role of morphosyntactic headedness in rhythmic patterning of reduplicative words.
column7: Phuong Dang(The Ohio State University)

column4: Can Hands Articulate? Kinematic, Acoustic, and Perceptual Analyses of Vowel Production via External Resonators in Kaxi
column6: The source-filter model is foundational in speech science, but the potential for external filters to replace the vocal tract remains underexplored. This research investigates Kaxi, a Chinese folk art in which a reed serves as the source and hand movements act as an external resonator. Kinematic, acoustic, and perceptual analyses of five Kaxi vowels were performed to determine whether hands can articulate intelligible speech. Kinematic tracking reveals that hand postures create a distinct spatial map analogous to tongue-based vowel spaces. Acoustically, Kaxi employs a staircase-like formant tuning strategy to maintain vowel distinctiveness despite high fundamental frequencies. Perceptual evaluations with 24 listeners demonstrate relative robust intelligibility. These results confirm that hands can function effectively as an external speech filter, offering insights into speech plasticity and presenting a potential non-invasive tool for clinical speech rehabilitation.
column7: Jinyang Ren(Peking University); Bingliang Zhao(Peking University); Jiangping Kong(Peking University); Xiyu Wu(Peking University)

column4: Naming Heroes and Villains – The Influence of Phonaesthetics
column6: In constructed languages, creators often represent the personality or character traits of a fictional people linguistically through phonaesthetics, e.g., Tolkien's Orkish, developed to sound harsh and evil, vs. the Elvish languages Sindarin and Quenya, designed to sound elegant and pleasant. The present study investigates whether these design principles are applied to the creation of character names for fictional heroes and villains in German. Participants were asked to invent names for good or evil fictional characters based on two syllable-sized building blocks they selected out of four alternatives. These syllables varied in levels of sonority, nucleus length and CV-complexity. Results show significant differences between the characteristics of syllables selected for naming good and evil characters. GLMERs show significant effects of character (good or evil) on the sonority of syllables selected for naming as well as an influence of the other selected syllable's sonority.
column7: Leonie Schade(Bielefeld University); Daniel Duran(Bielefeld University); Florian Kankowski(Bielefeld University); Joana Cholin(Bielefeld University); Petra Wagner(Bielefeld University); Christine Mooshammer(Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin)

column4: The Perception of Korean Stop Coda Consonants by Mandarin Speakers in Taiwan: A Comparative Study of Proficiency Levels
column6: This study investigates the perceptual identification of Korean stop codas (/p, t, k/) by Mandarin speakers in Taiwan, focusing on preceding vowel context and learning experience. Motivated by reports that these learners often produce Korean unreleased codas with audible release, a four-alternative coda identification task was conducted with 30 learners (17 beginners, 13 intermediate learners). Results showed an accuracy hierarchy of /p/ > /t/ > /k/. Vowel context shaped accuracy and confusion patterns: /p/ was best identified after /i/ and /u/, /t/ was best identified after /a/, /t/ was often misperceived as /k/ after non-front vowels (/a, u/), and /k/ showed vowel-dependent confusions. Proficiency group did not significantly affect accuracy, indicating no reliable beginner-intermediate difference in the present sample and task. These findings suggest the need for targeted perceptual training that integrates vowel context and unreleased coda contrasts in Korean teaching.
column7: Shu-Wei Yang(Seoul National University); Jung-yueh Tu(National Chengchi University)

column4: Returning the Turn: Do Backchannels Pattern More Like Turn-Holds or Turn-Changes Given Preceding Syntactic Completion and Boundary Tones?
column6: Backchannels are short listener response tokens such as "uh-huh" and "yeah" that signal understanding and encourage the speaker to go on. Several backchannel-inviting cues have been identified in the speech signal directly preceding backchannels, including low and rising final intonation. Since studies on intonation and turn-taking in Dutch have previously treated backchannels as a subclass of turn holds, backchannel-inviting cues in Dutch still lack clarity. The present study re-examines the place of backchannels in the turn-taking system of Dutch based on their cues, asking the question of whether they more closely resemble turn holds or changes in terms of immediately preceding boundary tones and syntactic completion. The results show that backchannels pattern differently from both turn holds and changes, while showing a relatively closer resemblance to the latter category.
column7: Ariëlle Reitsema(Leiden University); Matthijs Westera(Leiden University); Yiya Chen(Leiden University); Johanneke Caspers(Leiden University)

column1: Tuesday 29 September 2026 - 14:00-16:00 - Area 4 - Poster 6 - Spoofing and Deepfake Detection 2

column4: Improving Generalization in Speech Deepfake Detection via Orthogonality-Constrained Common-Specific Feature Decorrelation
column6: Advances in deep learning-based Text-to-Speech (TTS) and Voice Conversion (VC) have enabled highly realistic speech deepfakes, posing serious threats such as fraud and misinformation. Although end-to-end deepfake detection models like RawNet2, RawGAT-ST, and AASIST have been proposed, they often overfit to dataset-specific artifacts under empirical risk minimization. To improve generalization, we propose an orthogonality-based feature decorrelation method for SSL-AASIST, which learns domain-invariant common features that capture consistent authenticity cues and attack-specific specialized features, together with an orthogonality regularization that minimizes their correlation. This encourages the model to rely on consistent authenticity cues rather than domain-dependent shortcuts. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves lower EERs than the baseline across unseen corpora such as 21DF, ASV5, and ITW, confirming improved robustness to unseen domains and spoofing attacks.
column7: Donghee Kim(Incheon National University); Wooil Kim(Incheon National University)

column4: Task-Aware Joint Pruning and Distillation for Efficient Audio Deepfake Detection
column6: Advances in speech synthesis have made deepfake speeches increasingly convincing, posing growing threats to security. While self-supervised learning (SSL) based detectors achieve state-of-the-art performance, their computational demands (typically 300M+ parameters) prevent deployment on resource-constrained devices. Existing compression methods, designed mainly for content-centric tasks, struggle to maintain competitive performance when directly adapted to deepfake detection. We propose a Task-Aware Joint Pruning and Distillation framework that combines cross-domain knowledge distillation with movement-guided structured pruning to transfer forgery-discriminative knowledge and preserve critical structures under aggressive compression. Our framework reduces the model to 31.9M parameters with 6.3x FLOPs reduction, with an average performance drop of only 1.30% across multiple datasets compared to the uncompressed baseline, demonstrating strong potential for on-device deployment.

column4: ADD-DINO: A Two-Stage Self-Distillation Framework for Audio Deepfake Detection
column6: This paper proposes ADD-DINO, a two-stage framework aimed at alleviating label scarcity and improving cross-domain generalization in audio deepfake detection. In the first stage, the model is pretrained in a self-supervised manner on 1 million unlabeled audio samples using a non-contrastive teacher-student self-distillation scheme: the teacher branch takes a global long segment, the student branch takes a noise-augmented local short segment, and global-local consistency is learned by aligning their representations. In the second stage, the pretrained teacher backbone is fine-tuned on labeled data for the detection task. Experiments show that on ASVspoof 2019 LA, ADD-DINO achieves performance comparable to a fully supervised baseline using only 20% of the labeled data, and exhibits stronger crossdomain generalization on benchmarks such as In-the-Wild and DFADD. For unseen synthesis methods (e.g., CosyVoice and F5-TTS), ADD-DINO yields a 19.99% relative reduction in EER and a 22.7% improvement in accuracy over the baseline.

column4: FakeSound2: A Benchmark for Explainable, Traceable, and Generalizable Deepfake Sound Detection
column6: The growth of audio generation has brought ethical and security concerns over deepfakes, making deepfake detection critical to preventing the malicious misuse of such technologies. Existing methods largely focus on binary classification but fall short in explaining how audio is manipulated, tracing origins, or generalizing to unseen sources, limiting the explainability and reliability of detection. To address these issues, we present FakeSound2, a benchmark designed to advance deepfake sound detection beyond binary accuracy. It evaluates models across three dimensions: localization, traceability, and generalization, covering 6 manipulation types and 12 sources. Experiments reveal that existing models struggle to recognize forgery patterns, provide reliable explanations, and generalize well. FakeSound2 serves as a comprehensive benchmark that highlights key challenges and promotes the development of explainable, traceable, and generalizable methods for trustworthy audio authentication.
column7: Zeyu Xie(Peking University; Tencent AI Lab); Yaoyun Zhang(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Xuenan Xu(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Yongkang Yin(Peking University); Chenxing Li(Tencent AI Lab); Mengyue Wu(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Yuexian Zou(Peking University)

column4: Evidence Subspace Projection: Measuring How Much Evidence Explains Deepfake Detection in Self-Supervised Speech Models
column6: Self-supervised learning (SSL) models are widely used as feature extractors for state-of-the-art audio deepfake detection, but it remains unclear how to directly and quantitatively connect what SSL models capture to detection decisions. To address this gap, we propose Evidence Subspace Projection, a method that represents both evidence factors (e.g., attack category, codec, gender, transmission) and authenticity labels in a shared space constructed from SSL models' neuron activation patterns. By projecting the decision vector onto each evidence subspace, we obtain a scalar ratio that quantifies the explanatory power of each evidence type. We evaluate SSL models in raw, fine-tuned, and post-trained settings on multiple datasets. The results confirm findings from established studies, validating the proposed method, and reveal new insights into model behavior.
column7: Yixuan Xiao(University of Stuttgart); Cheng-Wei Lin(University of Stuttgart); Xin Wang(National Institute of Informatics); Yassine El Kheir(German Research Center for Artificial Intelligence (DFKI)); Arnab Das(German Research Center for Artificial Intelligence (DFKI)); Tim Polzehl(German Research Center for Artificial Intelligence (DFKI)); Sebastian Möller(Technical University of Berlin); Ngoc Thang Vu(University of Stuttgart)

column4: Towards Robust Speech Deepfake Detection via Human-Inspired Reasoning
column6: The modern generative audio models can be used by an adversary in an unlawful manner, specifically, to impersonate other people to gain access to private information. To mitigate this issue, speech deepfake detection (SDD) methods started to evolve. Unfortunately, current SDD methods generally suffer from the lack of generalization to new audio domains and generators. More than that, they lack interpretability, especially human-like reasoning that would naturally explain the attribution of a given audio to the bona fide or spoof class and provide human-perceptible cues. In this paper, we propose HIR-SDD, a novel SDD framework that combines the strengths of Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) with the chain-of-thought reasoning derived from the novel proposed human-annotated dataset. Experimental evaluation demonstrates both the effectiveness of the proposed method and its ability to provide reasonable justifications for predictions.
column7: Artem Dvirniak(MIRAI); Evgeny Kushnir(AXXX; HSE; Applied AI Institute); Dmitrii Tarasov(HSE; Applied AI Institute); Artem Iudin(MTUCI); Oleg Kiriukhin(City University of Hong Kong); Mikhail Pautov(AXXX; Trusted AI Research Center); Dmitrii Korzh(AXXX; Applied AI Institute; MTUCI); Oleg Rogov(AXXX; Applied AI Institute; MTUCI)

column4: Physics-Aware Deepfake Detection via Distance–Speech Consistency
column6: Recent progress in generative models has made talking-head deepfakes highly realistic and easy to create, jeopardizing public trust. However, most audio-visual deepfake detectors rely on lip-speech synchronization and are designed for static, frontal videos, limiting their reliability in dynamic, in-the-wild recordings where the speaker moves and lip cues are degraded or missing. As an alternative, we propose a physics-aware detector for dynamic speaking videos that leverages an acoustic constraint: in real recordings, speech energy varies predictably with speaker-to-camera distance, whereas deepfake generation can break this coupling. Our method combines distance estimates from video with distance-dependent acoustic measures from speech to detect deepfakes. Experiments on in-the-wild benchmarks show that the proposed physical cue is effective in dynamic scenarios, and that it complements lip-sync-based detectors, with a simple ensemble achieving consistent gains across datasets. Codes are available at https://byulharang.github.io/PADD/.
column7: Kyeongrae Kim(KAIST); Kim Sung-Bin(POSTECH); Oh Hyun-Bin(POSTECH); Tae-Hyun Oh(KAIST)

column4: MS-GNN: Multi-Scale Graph Neural Network for Detecting Local Audio-Visual Forgery Traces
column6: The proliferation of audio-visual deepfake technology poses a threat to social trust. Approaches relying on globally pooled multimodal features can dilute transient forgery traces (e.g., lip-sync misalignments). We propose MS-GNN, a multi-scale graph neural network for audio-visual deepfake detection. MS-GNN partitions the audio-visual stream into windows to capture local traces. We use a multi-scale graph: a bottom-up pathway aggregates window features into segment-level semantics, while a top-down pathway propagates global context to refine local evidence. We obtain a global video representation by aggregating window features, and train with window-level (auxiliary) and video-level (main) supervision. Experiments on LAV-DF and FakeAVCeleb show that MS-GNN improves deepfake detection, particularly for videos with localized forgery traces. The source code will be available here.
column7: Jianrong Wang(Tianjin University; Tianjin Renai College); Hengyang Guo(Tianjin University); Jie Liu(Tianjin Electronic Information College); Ju Zhang(Tianjin University of Technology); Qi Li(Tianjin University); Ying Guo(Tianjin University); Jing Zhao(Tianjin Beiyang Rongke Intelligent Technology Co., Ltd.)

column4: Referee: Reference-aware Audiovisual Deepfake Detection
column6: Deepfakes have rapidly posed serious threats from advanced generative models, yet audiovisual deepfake detection approaches still struggle to generalize to unseen manipulation methods. We propose a novel reference-aware audiovisual deepfake detection method, called Referee, to capture fine-grained identity discrepancies. Referee employs identity bottleneck and matching modules to model the relational consistency of speaker-specific cues captured by a single one-shot example as a biometric anchor. Extensive experiments on FakeAVCeleb, FaceForensics++, and KoDF demonstrate that Referee achieves state-of-the-art results on cross-dataset and cross-language evaluation protocols. These results highlight that explicitly correlating reference-based biometric priors is a key frontier for achieving reliable audiovisual forensics. The code is available at https://github.com/ewha-mmai/referee.
column7: Hyemin Boo(Ewha Womans University); Eunsang Lee(Ewha Womans University); Jiyoung Lee(Ewha Womans University)

column4: OPERA-Net: Octave-aware Phase-sensitive Enhanced Recognition Architecture for Singing Voice Deepfake Detection
column6: The proliferation of high-fidelity singing voice synthesis requires robust Singing Voice Deepfake Detection (SVDD) countermeasures. However, state-of-the-art speech spoofing detectors degrade significantly when applied to singing. This vulnerability arises from dense background music (BGM) interference and reliance on magnitude spectra, which discard critical phase discontinuities. To address these, we propose OPERA-Net, a novel dual-stream architecture for SVDD. We introduce a Phase-Consistent CQT (PC-CQT) representation that models instantaneous frequency derivatives to capture phase anomalies. A Semantic-Guided Gating mechanism leverages pre-trained WavLM semantic priors to filter the PC-CQT stream, isolating vocal forgery traces from BGM. Cross-corpus evaluations on the CtrSVDD and SingFake datasets show OPERA-Net achieves state-of-the-art performance, with superior generalization over existing baselines.
column7: Fengwei Ye(Sun Yat-sen University); Kun Zeng(Sun Yat-sen University)

column4: A Training-Free Proactive Defense Against Partial Speech Manipulation via Self-Embedding Steganography
column6: Partial deepfake speech, where only limited segments of an utterance are synthesized or manipulated, poses a significant challenge to existing deepfake detection systems. As the proportion of spoofed regions decreases, passive detectors become increasingly unreliable, and accurate detection and restoration remain challenging. In this paper, we revisit audio steganography from a new perspective and propose its use as a proactive defense against partially deepfaked audio. In particular, we consider a self-embedding strategy in which a clean speech signal embeds a compressed representation of itself, enabling post-hoc extraction of reference content. We demonstrate how existing audio steganography methods can be repurposed to support detection of partial deepfakes through codec-based restoration. Experiments on a benchmark dataset show that the proposed approach complements passive defenses. Remarkably, the proposed method operates without any training, providing a robust and data-efficient alternative for partial deepfake detection.
column7: Yigitcan Özer(National Institute of Informatics); Zhe Zhang(National Institute of Informatics); Wanying Ge(National Institute of Informatics); Xin Wang(National Institute of Informatics); Junichi Yamagishi(National Institute of Informatics)

column4: Consistency-Regularized Dual-Branch Network with Performance-Aware Mean Teacher for Sound Event Detection
column6: In this paper, we introduce a method to enhance pre-trained model-based sound event detection. The model architecture consists of a pre-trained Audio Teacher Student Transformer (ATST) front-end and a cascaded dual-branch back-end that models shallow and deep features of ATST, respectively. To capture more discriminative cues, we propose a temporal topological consistency loss to align the temporal structural similarities of the dual-branch features. For model training, we propose a performance-aware mean teacher framework, which features an adaptive exponential moving average strategy to adjust the teacher model's update magnitude based on the student model's performance, thereby ensuring the stability of model updates. Furthermore, we employ a cross-stage fusion strategy to combine the strengths of different training stages. Experimental results on the DCASE 2024 Challenge Task 4 dataset demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method.
column7: Lipeng Dai(University of Science and Technology of China); Qing Wang(University of Science and Technology of China); Wu Guo(University of Science and Technology of China); Peng Gao(University of Science and Technology of China); Zhijun Zhang(University of Science and Technology of China); Kuiliang Li(University of Science and Technology of China); Jinjie Fu(University of Science and Technology of China)

column4: MixProLAP: Mixture-Induced Uncertainty Modeling for Probabilistic Language-Audio Pretraining
column6: Acoustic environments often contain multiple overlapping sound events, and the same acoustic scene can be described using diverse textual expressions, making audio-text alignment inherently ambiguous. This paper proposes a probabilistic audio-language pretraining framework to model many-to-many correspondence ambiguity in audio-text alignment. Unlike conventional contrastive methods that learn deterministic point embeddings, our approach represents each modality as a distribution and learns uncertainty-aware cross-modal alignment. Rather than relying on masking-based uncertainty simulation, we mix audio-text pairs to create overlapping sounds that better reflect real acoustic mixtures and capture semantic inclusion relations among sound events. We further introduce a multi-level inclusion loss to enforce representations consistent with these relations. Experiments on audio-text retrieval benchmarks show that the proposed method outperforms deterministic baselines.
column7: Yu Nakagome(LINE WORKS Corporation); Jaesong Lee(NAVER Cloud Corporation); Soo-Whan Chung(NAVER Cloud Corporation)

column4: UD-ASD: A Unified Diffusion Model for Anomalous Sound Detection
column6: Anomalous Sound Detection (ASD) aims to determine whether faults have occurred by monitoring sounds. Existing methods detect a limited range of anomalies, exhibit poor generalization, or train a separate model for each machine. Diffusion models possess strong generalization and can generate specific data with condition guidance. We propose a unified diffusion model only with a small module. The audio is first transformed into log-Mel spectrograms. The lightweight module embeds machine IDs into condition embeddings, guiding the model to reconstruct data for specific machines. Then diffusion model reconstructs data with condition, using Gaussian Mixture Models to fit the distributions of reconstruction errors. Our unified model could monitor multiple machine types and learn more fundamental feature spaces with cross-domain learning. Experiments on DCASE2022 Challenge Task 2 show that our model achieves 3.44% AUC and 2.52% pAUC improvements over baseline, validating its effectiveness.
column7: Pengxiang Gao(University of Science and Technology of China); Yu Qiu(University of Science and Technology of China); Yanzhi Song(University of Science and Technology of China)

column4: A Semantic-Anchor-based Method for Open-Vocabulary Sound Event Detection
column6: Recent query-based open-vocabulary sound event detection (SED) is promising beyond closed-set models. Yet most methods only use query vectors for retrieval without semantic understanding of events, thus limiting recognition of novel classes. To tackle this, we propose a semantic-anchor-based method. Specifically, we learn a set of semantic anchor vectors to serve as semantic-level reference tokens, so arbitrary events can be better understood by attending to the anchors. We also introduce bidirectional-attention to enhance query-feature interaction for more effective retrieval, and design tailored query augmentation to improve robustness. Experiments on AudioSet-Strong show superior accuracy in recognizing novel classes, achieving 34.9 PSDS under the open-vocabulary setting and surpassing prior open-vocabulary SED models. Moreover, cross-dataset evaluation on DESED validates our method's strong generalization, and notably in zero-shot, we achieve 44.1 PSDS1, even surpassing DESED-supervised baseline.
column7: Jun Liu(University of Science and Technology of China); Pengfei Cai(University of Science and Technology of China); Yanfeng Shi(University of Science and Technology of China); Qing Gu(University of Science and Technology of China); Nan Jiang(University of Science and Technology of China); Lirong Dai(University of Science and Technology of China); Yan Song(University of Science and Technology of China)

column4: Cross Domain Few-Shot Class-Incremental Audio Classification Via Adversarial Contrastive Learning
column6: Current Few-shot Class-incremental Audio Classification (FCAC) methods assume that samples of base and incremental classes are in the same domain (following the same distribution). However, there is generally a domain shift between the above two types of samples. In this paper, we explore the problem of Cross Domain FCAC where samples of base and incremental classes have domain shift. We propose a strategy of adversarial contrastive training which enables the model to effectively classify samples of different classes from unseen domains. The model consists of an encoder and a classifier. The encoder is trained in base session but frozen in incremental sessions, whereas the classifier is trained in all sessions. Experiments are done on six pairs of cross-domain datasets. Results show that our method exceeds state-of-the-art methods in average accuracy. The code is at https://github.com/YongjieSi/ACL.
column7: Yongjie Si(South China University of Technology); Yanxiong Li(South China University of Technology); Sen Huang(South China University of Technology); Beibei Liu(South China University of Technology)

column4: USV-DETR: High-Resolution and Densely Supervised Detection of Ultrasonic Vocalizations
column6: Ultrasonic vocalizations (USVs) are important behavioral indicators in rodent neuroscience research, yet automated detection remains challenging due to their small scale, narrow bandwidth, and sparse distribution in spectrograms. Existing methods mostly rely on rule-based tools or traditional convolutional networks, which struggle to preserve critical acoustic details and lack effective mechanisms for modeling fine-grained and sparse acoustic patterns. We propose USV-DETR, an end-to-end model optimized for USV detection. Built on RT-DETR, it introduces a high-resolution P2 feature layer to better represent narrowband, short-duration signals and adopts the DEIM training framework to provide dense and stable supervision for sparse small targets. Experiments across different datasets show that USV-DETR consistently achieves the best detection performance, enabling more precise time-frequency localization of USVs and providing a useful tool for acoustic feature analysis.
column7: Yilan Wei(Northwestern University); Kumiko Long(Northwestern University); Arielle Granston(Northwestern University); Adrian Rodriguez-Contreras(Northwestern University)

column4: Enhancing Temporal Prediction Consistency for Short-Duration Acoustic Scene Classification via Semantic Adversarial Training
column6: Short-duration Acoustic Scene Classification (ASC) is essential for building responsive environmental sensing systems. However, standard ASC models show severe performance collapse when restricting to short observation windows. Our study reveals that the degradation stems from temporal prediction inconsistency--a misalignment between the long-term scene context and the model's predictions among short observation windows. To address this, we propose the Semantic Adversarial Training (SAT) framework. SAT introduces an auxiliary adversarial objective that competes with the standard scene classification task, forcing the feature extractor to discard duration-dependent semantic variances while learning scene-discriminative features. Experimental results demonstrate a direct correlation between temporal prediction consistency and model accuracy. Crucially, SAT significantly mitigates the performance drop on high-discrepancy samples, yielding a more robust and temporally consistent ASC system.
column7: Yiqiang Cai(Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University); Yizhou Tan(Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University); Peihong Zhang(Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University); Yuxuan Liu(Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University); Shengchen Li(Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University); Xi Shao(Nanjing University of Posts and Telecommunications)

column4: BG-CRNN: Boundary-Guided Dynamic Attention for Sound Event Detection in Complex Scenarios
column6: Existing sound event detection (SED) systems often suffer severe performance degradation in complex noisy environments. To address this, we propose a noise-robust Boundary-Guided Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network (BG-CRNN). We introduce a dynamic boundary attention module that constructs masks by predicting event boundaries. This restricts self-attention strictly within individual event segments, preventing target sound features from being contaminated by adjacent background noise. Furthermore, a Boundary-Guided Attention (BGA) module utilizes these boundary features to generate gating weights, adaptively enhancing active event regions. Experiments on the WildDESED dataset demonstrate that BG-CRNN consistently outperforms baselines across signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) from 10 dB to -5 dB. Notably, it achieves a PSDS1 of 0.191 even under the extreme -5 dB condition, confirming its strong noise robustness.
column7: Zongmu Lin(Wuhan University); Zhongxin Bai(Harbin Engineering University); Jisheng Bai(Xi'an University of Posts and Telecommunications); Zhenru Li(Wuhan University); Ting Dang(University of Melbourne); Gongping Huang(Wuhan University); Jingdong Chen(Northwestern Polytechnical University); Jacob Benesty(University of Quebec)

column4: Towards Event-Robust Acoustic Scene Classification
column6: This paper introduces the Event-Shifted Acoustic Scene (ESAS) dataset, a novel benchmark for evaluating the robustness of Acoustic Scene Classification (ASC) systems against unknown sound events. Existing ASC datasets typically contain recordings of clean and consistent audio, while real-world environments often include diverse and unexpected sound events. To bridge this gap, ESAS simulates real-world acoustic variability by injecting foreground sound events into background scenes with the assistance of large language models. In this work, we present the construction methodology, dataset statistics, and evaluation protocols. Furthermore, a comprehensive evaluation of state-of-the-art ASC systems is conducted using the ESAS benchmark. Experimental results reveal that existing ASC models suffer significant performance degradation when facing the event-shift challenge. The introduction of the ESAS dataset aims to drive future research toward event-robust ASC.
column7: Yiqiang Cai(Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University); Bohan Hu(Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University); Yu Yang(Zhongdian Zhiheng Information Technology Service Co., Ltd); Pengwei Lu(China Telecom Jiangsu Branch); Shengchen Li(Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University); Xi Shao(Nanjing University of Posts and Telecommunications)

column4: From Masking to Merging: Rethinking SpecAugment for Efficient Audio Spectrogram Transformer
column6: This paper proposes SpecAugment-Patch Merging, a simple yet effective method to accelerate Audio Spectrogram Transformer (AST) training. We first apply SpecAugment to mask input spectrograms at the patch level, and after positional embeddings are added, the method selects r pairs of masked patches and merges them, reducing the number of tokens processed by the Transformer. Increasing the number of merged pairs r from 0 to 100 keeps mAP on AudioSet nearly unchanged (34.07 to 34.08) while throughput increases from 43.3 to 49.3 samples/sec, which is a relatively 13.9% improvement. Similar patterns appear on ESC-50 and Speech Commands V2, where throughput steadily improves with only minor accuracy changes, demonstrating that this merging approach provides faster training with minimal performance loss.
column7: Minhee Park(Korea University); Hyowon Ahn(Korea University); Chanwoo Kim(Korea University)

column4: Progressive Learnable Counterfactual Attention for Music Classification
column6: Counterfactual attention learning mitigates biased attention by disentangling task-relevant cues from spurious regions. Learnable Counterfactual Attention (LCA) introduces a learnable counterfactual branch to expose misleading yet discriminative biases during training. However, learning in a single representation space often leaves residual biases entangled with the main attention. We propose Progressive Learnable Counterfactual Attention (P-LCA), a multi-stage framework that refines attention via stage-wise representation projection. After each counterfactual training stage, main-branch attention features are projected into a new latent space, allowing subsequent stages to examine biases from different perspectives and reveal hidden patterns. This design enables thorough and stable debiasing. Experiments on Artist20, GTZAN, and EMOPIA datasets show consistent improvements across music classification tasks, while attention visualizations indicate focused, stable attention patterns.
column7: Yi-Xing Lin(Academia Sinica); Wen-Li Wei(Academia Sinica); Jia-Ching Wang(National Central University); Jen-Chun Lin(Academia Sinica)

column4: Energy Redistribution in the Spectro-Temporal Modulation Domain for Near-End Listening Enhancement
column6: Near-end listening enhancement (NELE) improves speech intelligibility by modifying speech prior to playback in noisy environments. We propose a NELE algorithm that redisributes speech energy in the spectro-temporal modulation domain rather than the conventional time-frequency domain. A global modulation mask is optimized using an objective measure of speech intelligibility and applied under an energy constraint. An ablation study shows that jointly modifying spectral and temporal modulations results in more consistent gains than single-dimension masking. Evaluation on several noise types demonstrates consistent improvements over established NELE baselines across multiple objective and subjective measures of speech intelligibility.
column7: Amin Edraki(Huawei CBG); Amirhossein Hajavi(Huawei CBG); Irina Kezele(Huawei CBG); Yuanhao Yu(Huawei CBG)

column4: End-to-End Model Compression for Personalized Neural Speech Codecs
column6: Neural speech coding (NSC) leverages deep learning to achieve high-quality speech compression, surpassing conventional methods. However, recent NSC models have grown substantially in size and complexity, limiting their feasibility for real-time processing on resource-constrained devices. To address this issue, we propose a speaker-aware model compression framework for end-to-end NSC. In this approach, speakers are clustered by perceptual similarity, and both encoder and decoder are trained with group-specific data, reducing computation while preserving perceptual quality. Subjective listening tests show that the proposed method reduces the model size by 96% and the bitrate by 50% (from 2 kbps to 1 kbps), while maintaining the perceptual quality of the state-of-the-art Descript audio codec (DAC). Moreover, the personalized models remain robust under noisy conditions, consistently outperforming baselines under acoustic distortions. These results highlight the feasibility of deploying NSC on low-power devices in both clean and noisy environments.
column7: Inseon Jang(ETRI); Minje Kim(UIUC); Wootaek Lim(ETRI); Seungkwon Beack(ETRI)

column4: Acoustic and Semantic Feature Fusion Mapping for Lyric Intelligibility Prediction
column6: Lyric intelligibility, the ease with which listeners understand song lyrics, affects listening experience, memorability, and language learning. We propose a data-driven system extracting acoustic features, and Whisper encoder representations. Feature engineering, including temporal statistics and interactions among correlated features, enhances prediction. A regression module maps features to intelligibility scores using neural models (FCNs, MOE, CNN+GRU, Transformers) and gradient-boosted trees (CatBoost, LightGBM, XGBoost). Experiments on a manually annotated dataset show gradient-boosted trees outperform neural networks, with CatBoost achieving Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) 27.367 and correlation (Corr) 0.654. Results highlight the effectiveness of structured feature modeling and Whisper-derived representations.
column7: Yuxiang Fu(Tsinghua University); Guodong Lin(Tsinghua University); Da Shen(Tsinghua University); Wenlin Huang(Ministry of Public Security); Weili Jiang(Ministry of Public Security); Kai Gao(Ministry of Public Security); Boyu Zhao(Ministry of Public Security); Wei-Qiang Zhang(Tsinghua University)

column4: Screening Matters: A Comparative Study of Conventional and Crowdsourced Listening Tests
column6: Subjective evaluation remains the most reliable way of testing speech and audio coding techniques. Crowdsourcing the listening task is a cost-efficient and fast way of conducting this evaluation, but the quality of the results tends to be inferior to that of conventional listening tests done in the controlled environment of a laboratory. In this paper, classical and neural speech codecs are evaluated to compare P.808 against P.800 DCR tests. A statistical analysis is conducted to investigate the effectiveness of selected screening methods. The analysis shows that the crowdsourced evaluation can be improved by employing post-screening methods based on anchor ordering and rating span, and continuous screening methods like traps and gold standard questions, thus giving more value to the ratings obtained for the codecs under test. Based on these outcomes, a set of suitable screenings is proposed, for cost-effective, simplified, and bias-free enhancement of listening results.
column7: Anika Treffehn(Fraunhofer-Institut für Integrierte Schaltungen IIS); Andrea Eichenseer(Fraunhofer-Institut für Integrierte Schaltungen IIS); Emily Kratsch(Fraunhofer-Institut für Integrierte Schaltungen IIS); Nicola Pia(Fraunhofer-Institut für Integrierte Schaltungen IIS)

column4: Assessing the Impact of Noise and Speech Enhancement on the Intelligibility of Speech Codecs
column6: Preserving speech intelligibility is a minimum requirement for speech codecs in communication. Recently, very low-bitrate neural codecs have gained interest for replacing classical codecs, reinforcing the need to evaluate whether intelligibility is preserved in realistic scenarios. In this paper, we evaluate the intelligibility and listening effort of classical and neural speech codecs in clean and noisy conditions. Further, we assess the impact of speech enhancement (SE) before coding, simulating a possible audio processing pipeline. The results show that classical codecs are more noise robust than neural codecs. Further, SE can lead to significant intelligibility and listening effort improvements for codecs otherwise negatively affected by noise. Listening effort reveals nuanced differences when intelligibility is saturated. Lastly, objective intelligibility based on automatic speech recognition is highly correlated with subjective intelligibility scores averaged per condition.
column7: Lyonel Behringer(IIS); Anna Leschanowsky(Fraunhofer Institute for Integrated Circuits (IIS)); Anjana Rajasekhar(Fraunhofer Institute for Integrated Circuits (IIS)); Emily Kratsch(Fraunhofer Institute for Integrated Circuits (IIS)); Guillaume Fuchs(Fraunhofer Institute for Integrated Circuits (IIS))

column4: Improving Cross-Dataset Speech Intelligibility Prediction for Hearing-Impaired Listeners with Few-Shot Adaptation
column6: Speech intelligibility prediction models suffer substantial performance degradation when generalized to unseen datasets. In real-world scenarios, subjective listening evaluations are costly and limited, resulting in scarce labeled data for cross-dataset adaptation, which further challenges the development of accurate and generalizable evaluation models. To address this issue, we propose CFA-SIPNet, a speech intelligibility prediction network for hearing-impaired (HI) listeners based on cross-domain few-shot adaptation with adapter modules and contrastive learning. Experimental results show that CFA-SIPNet achieves a relative RMSE reduction of 8.5% and a relative PCC improvement of 4.2% over the state-of-the-art (SOTA) model in cross-dataset prediction. With less than 20% of target-domain samples, CFA-SIPNet outperforms models trained on the full in-domain target dataset. These results validate the effectiveness of CFA-SIPNet in enhancing cross-dataset generalization.
column7: Guojian Lin(Southern Univ. of Sci. and Tech.); Xuefei Wang(Southern Univ. of Sci. and Tech.); Ryandhimas E. Zezario(Academia Sinica); Yu Tsao(Academia Sinica); Fei Chen(Southern Univ. of Sci. and Tech.)

column4: Beyond Cross-Reconstruction: Probing-Based Disentanglement Evaluation for Acoustic Teleportation Codecs
column6: Some neural audio codecs disentangle speech into latent subspaces encoding content, speaker identity, and acoustics, enabling acoustic teleportation and voice conversion. Existing evaluations rely on cross-reconstruction quality, which cannot reliably detect leakage across partitions. We extend a probing-based framework to assess disentanglement by regressing room-acoustic parameters (reverberation time, clarity, and direct-to-reverberant ratio) and classifying speaker identity, using the gap between intended and unintended partitions as the disentanglement measure. Applied to an acoustic teleportation codec, we find speaker identity is largely confined to its partition, while acoustics leak into the speech embeddings due to the training objective. Acoustic embeddings blindly estimate room parameters within 0.02 s of supervised baselines, indicating physically meaningful structure emerges without explicit supervision.
column7: Philipp Grundhuber(Fraunhofer Institute for Integrated Circuits); Emanuël A. P. Habets(International Audio Laboratories Erlangen)

column4: Too Good to Be True: A Study on Modern Automatic Speech Recognition Systems for the Evaluation of Speech Enhancement
column6: Speech enhancement (SE) systems are typically evaluated using a variety of instrumental metrics. The use of automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems to evaluate SE performance is common in literature, usually in terms of word error rate (WER). However, WER scores depend heavily on the choice of ASR system and text normalization pipeline. In this paper, we investigate how modern ASR models correlate with human recognition of enhanced speech. A listening experiment reveals that modern ASR models with large-scale noisy training and embedded language models correlate more with human WER than simpler ones, with a transducer model providing the most reliable transcriptions. Nevertheless, we also show that these models' robustness to noise and use of context can be uninformative to an acoustics-focused evaluation of enhancement performance.
column7: Danilo Oliveira(University of Hamburg); Tal Peer(University of Hamburg); Timo Gerkmann(University of Hamburg)

column4: Probing Low Frame Rate Degradation in Neural Audio Codecs
column6: Low frame rates in neural audio codecs are attractive for autoregressive speech synthesis, where the generation cost scales linearly with the sequence length. Recent work has demonstrated that codecs can operate at 12.5 Hz and below, but the mechanisms underlying low frame rate degradation remain insufficiently understood. We investigate these mechanisms through a controlled frame rate ablation. We reproduce a quality cliff at 6.25 Hz reported in previous works and evaluate candidate explanations: phonemic collisions and codebook saturation, neither of which shows evidence of a fundamental barrier. The cliff is instead caused by suboptimal training configuration: fixed clip duration during training yields too few tokens at low frame rates, starving the decoder of inter-token context. Once corrected, WER degrades smoothly with phonemic load down to 3.1 Hz and 1.6 Hz, suggesting the inference-time efficiency gains of low frame rate codecs are more accessible than previously assumed.
column7: Alex Gichamba(Carnegie Mellon University Africa); Moise Busogi(Carnegie Mellon University Africa)
