column4: Deterministic Prompting for Speaker-Stable Low-Resource Greek TTS
column6: Modern TTS systems approach human quality for high-resource languages but degrade when clean speech data is scarce. Modern Greek exemplifies this, lacking the curated corpora behind state-of-the-art synthesis. We propose a data curation recipe that transforms audiobook recordings into TTS-ready data via WhisperX alignment and filtering. Then we fine-tune Parler-TTS (880M), a prompt-based multilingual model whose pretraining encodes phonetic priors transferable to Greek. During development, we find that LLM-generated style prompts introduce speaker drift at inference. Replacing them with deterministic prompts resolves this, and a speaker-specific LoRA stage trained on 3.5 h of single-speaker data anchors identity while updating ~5% of parameters. Our system achieves WER 10.7% (2.9 above the ASR floor), MOS-I 4.00 (vs. 4.36 human speech), and near-human speaker consistency (MOS-C 4.24 vs. 4.30), showing that robust single-speaker Greek TTS is achievable with limited curated data.
column7: Georgios Syllas(Athena R.C.); Efthymios Georgiou(University of Bern); Kosmas Kritsis(Athena R.C.); Alexandros Potamianos(National Technical University of Athens)

column4: DiaMoE-TTS: A Unified IPA-Based Dialect TTS Framework with Parameter-Efficient Adaptation and Reward-Driven Optimization
column6: Dialect speech embodies rich cultural and linguistic diversity, yet building a unified text-to-speech (TTS) system for dialects remains challenging due to scarce data, inconsistent phonetic representations, and dialect interference in joint modeling. We explore a unified dialect TTS pipeline based on a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) architecture. A unified International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) front-end is adopted to reduce pronunciation ambiguity across dialects. Built upon the F5-TTS framework, we introduce a dialect-aware Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) text encoder to mitigate style averaging in multidialect training. For low-resource dialect expansion, we employ parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) to enable adaptation with only a few hours of speech data. We further investigate incorporating high-quality dialect data into the unified model. Experiments show that GRPO-based reinforcement learning reduces the word error rate (WER) for both the target dialect and several related dialects.
column7: Ziqi Chen(Tsinghua University); Gongyu Chen(Giant Network); Yihua Wang(Giant Network); Zihao Chen(Giant Network); Wei-Qiang Zhang(Tsinghua University)

column4: SALT: Selective Allophone-Level Tokenization for Korean Text-to-Speech Synthesis
column6: Recent Korean TTS studies often use direct grapheme input due to the phonetic transparency of the Korean alphabet, Hangul. However, Korean orthography is also morphophonemic, and grapheme sequences do not always correspond to the actual pronunciation. Since the mapping between graphemes, phonemes, and allophones is almost deterministic in the Standard Korean Pronunciation, we propose Selective Allophone-Level Tokenization (SALT), which incorporates a selected set of allophonic phenomena into the input rather than relying on implicit learning by the TTS model. In experiments fine-tuning a pre-trained model, SALT-N, which improves token distributional balance, outperformed baselines. In a 12.75-hour dataset, SALT-N obtained a CER of 3.30% and achieved the highest NMOS, whereas grapheme input resulted in a CER of 4.74%. In an extremely low-resource 1-hour setting, SALT-N was the only method to achieve a CER below 10% (8.19%), whereas all baseline models suffered from severe degradation.
column7: Kwangsung Kim(CBS; Sogang University); Cellik Adams(Sogang University); EunKyoung Jo(Global Korean Studies, Sogang University)

column4: G2PO: A Lightweight Lexicon-enhanced Framework for Open-Vocabulary Mandarin Polyphone Disambiguation
column6: Polyphone disambiguation is a crucial component for Chinese Text-to-Speech systems. While recent arts achieve high accuracy using large pre-trained models like BERT, their massive parameter sizes hinder on-device deployment. Furthermore, these closed-set classifiers fail to predict pronunciations unseen during training. To address this, we propose g2pO, a lightweight open-vocabulary framework. It adopts a tiny BERT encoder and fuses external dictionary knowledge into hidden states via a lexicon adapter. Instead of using heavy pre-trained word embeddings to encode dictionary information, our method dynamically constructs word representations from hidden states via mix-pooling. These designs minimize the parameter size and enable generalization to unseen pronunciations. Experiments show with only 3.99M parameters (27x smaller than BERT-based methods), g2pO outperforms previous methods, achieving 99.15% accuracy on the CPP dataset and 70.79% zero-shot accuracy on unseen pronunciations.
column7: Feifan Chen(Samsung R&D Institute China-Beijing); Chunhui Lu(Samsung R&D Institute China-Beijing); Rui Zhou(Samsung R&D Institute China-Beijing); Liming Song(Samsung R&D Institute China-Beijing); Hongjun Kil(Mobile eXperience Business, Samsung Electronics); YoonChoon Hwang(Mobile eXperience Business, Samsung Electronics); Junkwang Oh(Mobile eXperience Business, Samsung Electronics)

column4: UR-BERT: Scaling Text Encoders for Massively Multilingual TTS Through Universal Romanization and Speech Token Prediction
column6: We propose UR-BERT, a Romanized transcription-based text-to-speech (TTS) encoder for massively multilingual TTS systems. Conventional grapheme-to-phoneme (G2P)-based approaches are limited to around 100 languages due to the availability of reliable G2P resources. In contrast, UR-BERT scales to 495 languages by unifying diverse writing systems into a shared Romanization representation. To further enhance phonetic fidelity and text-speech alignment, we introduce a speech token prediction objective during training, which encourages the encoder to learn speech-aware phonetic representations in a data-efficient manner. Experiments show that TTS systems built on UR-BERT consistently outperform recent text encoder baselines across a wide range of languages and resource conditions, and demonstrate strong generalization to unseen languages.
column7: Sangmin Lee(Yonsei University); Eek Gyun Ahn(Yonsei University); Woongjib Choi(Yonsei University); Hong-Goo Kang(Yonsei University)

column4: Listenability of Synthetic Speech: On the Effect of Linguistic Registers in Text-to-Speech Input
column6: With the rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs), LLM-generated text is increasingly being used as input for speech synthesis, yet little is known about its listenability compared to other linguistic registers. This paper presents a preliminary study of listenability across conversational, formal written, simplified written, and LLM-generated registers in terms of listener effort and comprehension during synthesized delivery. An experiment with 47 participants measured subjective mental effort, cognitive load, and cued recall in a within-subjects design. Register characteristics were examined through readability metrics and Biber's Multi-Dimensional Analysis. Our findings indicate higher listenability for synthesized speech from written sources compared to radio transcripts, demonstrating the intricacies of language and register. Furthermore, LLM-generated text was as listenable as Wikipedia-sourced text, supporting its suitability in synthetic speech applications.
column7: Maja Jønck Hjuler(Queensland University of Technology; Université Grenoble Alpes); Tuyet Katie Nhi Tran(Queensland University of Technology); Laurianne Sitbon(Queensland University of Technology)

column4: Uncovering the Impact of G2P Precision on Korean TTS: A Large-Scale Statistical Validation via a Novel Morphological Engine
column6: Grapheme-to-Phoneme (G2P) conversion is vital for TTS, yet the widely used Korean g2pk library suffers from high latency and inaccurate phonological modeling at word boundaries. Such inaccuracies act as "label noise", degrading TTS performance and training efficiency. To resolve this, we propose a novel rule-based G2P engine featuring an object-oriented data structure with syllable-morpheme connectivity and a recursive re-evaluation mechanism for sequential phonological rules. Rigorous benchmarking shows that the proposed engine significantly outperforms g2pk in both speed (3.14ms vs. 14.98ms, p < 0.001) and accuracy (85.7% vs. 27.2%). Furthermore, large-scale statistical validation via 96 VITS models (32 per condition) demonstrates that our engine achieves statistically significant improvements in intelligibility. The results confirm that our approach enhances not only the final audio quality but also the overall training efficiency of TTS models by providing consistent phonetic representations.
column7: Heejo You(Hyundai Motor Group); Sungwoo Moon(Hyundai Motor Group)

column4: Phonikud: Overcoming Phonetic Underspecification for Hebrew Text-To-Speech
column6: Text-to-speech (TTS) for Modern Hebrew is challenged by the language's orthographic complexity, with existing solutions ignoring underspecified phonetic features such as stress. We present a framework for more phonetically accurate Hebrew TTS with four contributions: (1) Phonikud, an open-source Hebrew grapheme-to-phoneme (G2P) system that outputs fully-specified International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) transcriptions, designed by augmenting a base diacritizer. (2) The ILSpeech corpus of paired Hebrew audio, text, and expert IPA annotations. (3) A benchmark for the previously unmeasured task of Hebrew G2P conversion. (4) Hebrew audio-to-IPA models capturing previously disregarded phonetic details for automatic TTS evaluation. Our results show that Phonikud more accurately predicts Hebrew phonemes than prior methods, and that small, local TTS models with phonetic input from Phonikud approach large proprietary systems. We release our code, data, and models at https://phonikud.github.io.
column7: Yakov Kolani(Independent Researcher); Maxim Melichov(Reichman University); Cobi Calev(Cisco Systems); Morris Alper(Tel Aviv University.; CMU)

column4: Speech-Worthy Alignment for Japanese SpeechLLMs via Direct Preference Optimization
column6: SpeechLLMs typically combine ASR-trained encoders with text-based LLM backbones, leading them to inherit written-style output patterns unsuitable for text-to-speech synthesis. This mismatch is particularly pronounced in Japanese, where spoken and written registers differ substantially in politeness markers, sentence-final particles, and syntactic complexity. We propose a preference-based alignment approach to adapt Japanese SpeechLLMs for speech-worthy outputs: text that is concise, conversational, and readily synthesized as natural speech. To rigorously evaluate this task, we introduce SpokenElyza, a benchmark for Japanese speech-worthiness derived from ELYZA-tasks-100 with auditory verification by a native expert. Experiments show that our approach achieves substantial improvement on SpokenElyza while largely preserving performance on the original written-style evaluation. We release SpokenElyza to support future research on Japanese spoken dialog systems.
column7: Mengjie Zhao(SB Intuitions); Lianbo Liu(SB Intuitions); Yusuke Fujita(SB Intuitions); Hao Shi(SB Intuitions); Yuan Gao(SB Intuitions); Roman Koshkin(SB Intuitions); Yui Sudo(SB Intuitions)

column4: Knowing What to Stress: A Discourse-Conditioned Text-to-Speech Benchmark
column6: Spoken meaning often depends not only on what is said, but also on which word is emphasized. The same sentence can convey correction, contrast, or clarification depending on where emphasis falls. Although modern text-to-speech (TTS) systems generate expressive speech, it remains unclear whether they infer contextually appropriate stress from discourse alone. To address this gap, we present Context-Aware Stress TTS (CAST), a benchmark for evaluating context-conditioned word-level stress in TTS. Items are defined as contrastive context pairs: identical sentences paired with distinct contexts requiring different stressed words. We evaluate state-of-the-art systems and find a consistent gap: text-only language models reliably recover the intended stress from context, yet TTS systems frequently fail to realize it in speech. We release the benchmark, evaluation framework, construction pipeline and a synthetic corpus to support future work on context-aware speech synthesis.
column7: Arnon Turetzky(The Hebrew University of Jerusalem); Avihu Dekel(IBM Research); Hagai Aronowitz(IBM Research); Ron Hoory(IBM Research); Yossi Adi(The Hebrew University of Jerusalem)

column4: Cross-Lingual Compositional Learning for Code-Switched Lip Reading
column6: Code-switching, the alternation of multiple languages in an utterance, is pervasive in multilingual communication but underexplored in visual speech recognition (VSR). Especially, the burden of collecting large-scale and realistic videos has limited the advances in code-switched VSR. We propose CoCoVSR, a cross-lingual compositional learning framework that exploits monolingual corpora. Specifically, without additional data collection or generative synthesis, CoCoVSR adapts a pretrained multilingual VSR model to code-switched scenarios, while preserving shared articulatory features. Experimental results show that CoCoVSR achieves SOTA on Chinese-English CSLR. Importantly, CoCoVSR achieves competitive performance on both seen (MultiVSR Chinese) and unseen (LRS2 English) multilingual datasets, highlighting its capability to preserve multilingual performance with negligible degradation. The code is available at https://github.com/ewha-mmai/CoCoVSR.
column7: Jeonghyeon Joo(Ewha Womans University); Jiyoung Lee(Ewha Womans University)

column4: Refining Pseudo-Audio Prompts with Speech-Text Alignment for Text-Only Domain Adaptation in LLM-Based ASR
column6: LLM-based automatic speech recognition models demonstrate strong performance by connecting audio encoders and LLMs. However, data scarcity of paired speech and transcription often hinders the adaptation to new domains, making text-only domain adaptation crucial. Existing methods typically rely on either fine-tuning the LLM alone or employing pseudo-audio prompts. The former neglects essential acoustic context, while the latter either suffers from limited scalability in data-scarce conditions, or yields inexpressive prompts by leveraging only textual features, ignoring audio modality. To address this, we propose a framework that explicitly models speech-text alignment. Our method efficiently generates highly expressive pseudo-audio prompts that bridge the modality gap, enabling effective target-domain adaptation. Experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing text-only methods, improving both overall error rates and out-of-vocabulary coverage.
column7: Ryo Magoshi(Kyoto University); Takashi Maekaku(LY Corporation); Yusuke Shinohara(LY Corporation)

column4: Content-Aware Dynamic Compression for Efffcient Speech Recognition based on Large Language Model
column6: Current LLM-based speech recognition systems use fixed-rate downsampling for acoustic representation, which overlooks speech content dynamics and causes information loss or redundancy. We propose a content-aware dynamic acoustic map-ping method via the Continuous Integrate-and-Fire (CIF) mechanism, adaptively aligning speech embeddings with transcription token counts. This enables content-guided downsampling during training and inference, cutting LLM input length while preserving or boosting accuracy. On AISHELL-1 and Lib-riSpeech, we achieve 12-26% relative error reduction at comparable average speech embedding length (ASEL). While main-taining comparable performance, we achieve over 45% ASEL reduction with 7-19% lower time to first token (TTFT) across utterance lengths. GigaSpeech results confirm scalability. Our work establishes an efficient paradigm improving the accuracy-efficiency trade-off in LLM-based speech recognition.
column7: Huifeng Zhu(BOE Technology Group Co., Ltd.); Bingqian Wang(BOE Technology Group Co., Ltd.); Shaoxun Xiu(BOE Technology Group Co., Ltd.); Xingqun Jiang(BOE Technology Group Co., Ltd.); Bin Lv(BOE Technology Group Co., Ltd.)

column4: Upcycling Pretrained Transformers into Mixture-of-Experts for Multilingual Speech Recognition
column6: Fine-tuning large pretrained models is a powerful way to obtain high-accuracy systems for downstream ASR tasks. However, when fine-tuning on highly diverse data, such as multilingual corpora, performance can degrade compared with training separate models per language, largely due to limited model capacity. In this paper, we propose a simple capacity expansion method for multilingual fine-tuning by upcycling the feed-forward network (FFN) components of a pretrained model into a post-hoc Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture. This conversion substantially increases the model's representational capacity while preserving inference efficiency: at test time, we activate only a single upcycled FFN expert, keeping the number of active parameters identical to the original dense model. We investigate two expert selection strategies: (1) hard routing based on language identity, and (2) soft routing using a learned router. Experiments on 10-language speech recognition with CommonVoice and additional ASR evaluations on four Asian languages demonstrate that the proposed upcycling-to-MoE approach consistently improves multilingual fine-tuning effectiveness.
column7: Kentaro Shinayama(NTT); Kohei Matsuura(NTT); Jaeyoung Lee(NTT); Masato Mimura(NTT)

column4: Token-Independent Language Representations for Low-Latency Configurable Multilingual Speech Recognition
column6: Configurable multilingual speech recognition enables a single model to be tailored to any user-selected language combination via language-specific modules (LSMs). While providing state-of-the-art accuracy, it incurs high latency as decoder LSMs are executed at every step, leading to extra computational costs that scale linearly with the output token length. To eliminate this per-token overhead, we propose token-independent language representations that decouple language identity from the autoregressive decoding loop. We replace the neural LSMs in the decoder with language representations enriched by one-time, utterance-level encoder cues. This reduces the LSM’s per-token complexity from quadratic to linear relative to the hidden dimension, while preserving utterance-level adaptability. Experiments show that our method achieves accuracy comparable to the original design while maintaining a near-constant LSM’s overhead, reducing peak inference latency by over 90% for long utterances.
column7: Hongxu Zhu(Fano); Lahiru Samarakoon(Fano); Ivan Fung(Fano)

column4: GC-LoRA: Gated Convolutional LoRA for Parameter-Efficient Acoustic Adaptation
column6: Transformer-based Speech Foundation Models excel in most Automatic Speech Recognition tasks but often suffer performance degradation when applied to domains with mismatched acoustic characteristics. While Parameter Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods, such as Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), adjust global attention, they lack the local context modeling crucial for capturing domain-specific variations. We propose GC-LoRA, a novel adapter architecture that injects Conformer-style local convolutional processing into pretrained Transformer encoders. By integrating a lightweight adapter to encoder attention output projections, our method efficiently captures local acoustic dependencies without disrupting pretrained global representations. Experiments across diverse datasets (acoustically-degraded, bandlimited, dialectal, child) demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, achieving Word Error Rate (WER) reductions of up to 10.9% compared to baselines while adding minimal trainable parameters.
column7: Natarajan Balaji Shankar(University of California Los Angeles); Zilai Wang(University of California Los Angeles); Kaiyuan Zhang(University of California Los Angeles); Mohan Shi(University of California Los Angeles); Abeer Alwan(University of California Los Angeles)

column4: MambAdapter: Lightweight Mamba-Based Adapters for Parameter-Efficient Transfer Learning in Speech and Audio
column6: Fine-tuning Transformer-based foundation models has become the dominant strategy for domain adaptation in audio and speech processing. To reduce the computational and memory costs of this process, parameter-efficient transfer learning (PETL) methods have been widely explored. Meanwhile, Mamba, a recent state-space model, has emerged as a promising alternative to Transformers for sequence modeling. In this work, we present MambAdapter, a parameter-efficient transfer learning approach that integrates Mamba into low-rank bottleneck adapters. Our design combines parameter sharing across adapters with the injection of a lightweight Mamba module, enabling more effective modeling of audio features. We demonstrate that MambAdapter matches or outperforms strong PETL baselines on four audio classification tasks and five speech recognition languages, even when operating under reduced parameter budgets.
column7: Salman Hussain Ali(Université de Montréal; Mila - Quebec AI Institute); Umberto Cappellazzo(Imperial College London); Mirco Ravanelli(Concordia University; Mila - Quebec AI Institute)

column4: PhonePrune: One-shot Phoneme-Aware Pruning for Large-scale ASR Models via Phoneme Set Generation and Calibration
column6: Large-scale Automatic Speech Recognition Models face deployment challenges due to massive parameter counts. While one-shot pruning compresses them, conventional methods indiscriminately discard low-magnitude parameters, degrading fine-grained phonetic distinctions. We conceptualize the sub-networks of these delicate weights as the Phoneme Ticket Hypothesis, arguing they must be preserved. We propose PhonePrune to preserve these weights via Phoneme Set Generation and Phoneme-aware Calibration. Evaluated on LibriSpeech and Common Voice (English, Korean, Japanese) at 50% sparsity, PhonePrune demonstrates strong results specifically on the Korean and Japanese datasets, yielding 13.41% and 13.83% Word Error Rate reductions over Distil-Whisper, respectively. Our success stems from preserving fragile parameters shared by these languages, such as subtle spectral variations in Korean and precise temporal durations in Japanese.
column7: Minsik Lee(Dongguk University); Jihie Kim(Dongguk University)

column4: Can Large Language Models Reliably Correct Errors in Low-Resource ASR? A Contamination-Aware Case Study on West Frisian
column6: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) has improved substantially in recent years, yet performance remains limited for low-resource languages. Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise for improving ASR through generative error correction (GER), but their effectiveness in low-resource settings remains underexplored. In addition, it remains unclear to what extent data contamination influences the reported improvements in LLM-based GER. This study investigates LLM-based GER for low-resource Frisian. In addition to a public corpus, we construct and use a Frisian offline dataset with non-public texts for evaluation to control for potential data contamination. Results show that GER improves ASR performance in most settings, with the best GPT-5.1 results surpassing oracle WERs. Comparable gains on the offline dataset indicate that improvements reflect true correction ability. We further provide a detailed error analysis revealing model correction patterns.
column7: Yun Hao(University of Groningen); Reihaneh Amooie(University of Groningen); Wietse de Vries(University of Groningen); Rik van Noord(University of Groningen); Martijn Wieling(University of Groningen)

column4: Contrastive Time-Proximity Pre-Training for Speech-Based Heart Failure Monitoring
column6: Heart failure (HF) causes recurrent acute decompensation (ADHF) requiring hospitalization. Fluid overload affects the vocal tract, making voice a potential non-invasive biomarker for early decompensation detection. Prior work used features from sustained vowels, relying on active patient engagement, limiting real-world applicability. We propose contrastive time-proximity (CTP), a self-supervised method learning HF-predictive representations from natural speech. CTP trains a segment-attentive LSTM to minimize embedding distances for recordings < 3 days apart (presumed similar health) while maximizing them for > 100 days apart (presumed different), exploiting HF's progressive nature. On a two-center dataset (68 ADHF patients), classical acoustic features achieve similar within-center accuracy but fail cross-center. CTP features suggest more robust cross-center generalization, outperforming random and human baselines. Attention analysis reveals focus on breathing-related segments.
column7: Tobias Fiedler(Noah Labs GmbH; University of Potsdam); Mariam Fouad(Noah Labs GmbH); Marcus Hott(Noah Labs GmbH); Leonhard Riehle(Noah Labs GmbH); Felix Hohendanner(German Heart Center of the Charité (DHZC)); Bruce Johnson(Mayo Clinic); Nicholas Cummins(King's College London); Bert Arnrich(University of Potsdam)

column4: Lung-CL: Spectrum-aware Distillation and Generative Replay for Continual Learning based buffer-free Respiratory Sound Classification
column6: Real-world respiratory sound classification faces performance degradation from domain shifts in heterogeneous clinical scenarios. While Continual Learning (CL) aims to alleviate catastrophic forgetting, it faces challenges regarding data privacy and the failure to handle audio-specific spectral characteristics. In this paper, we propose Lung-CL, a unified framework for buffer-free domain incremental respiratory sound classification. It incorporates a Class-Specific Latent Replay strategy that synthesizes pseudo-features from learned distributions, and a Multi-Level Spectrum-Aware Distillation mechanism that disentangles pathological patterns from domain-specific interference. Extensive experiments on three heterogeneous datasets (ICBHI, SPRSound and HF) show that Lung-CL significantly outperforms the existing continual learning methods in terms of classification accuracy and anti-forgetting ability.
column7: Qinben Lai(Hebei University of Technology); Lukui Shi(Hebei University of Technology); Jiaxin Zhao(Macao Polytechnic University); Wenjuan Wang(Hebei University of Technology); Shuai Liu(Hebei University of Technology)

column4: An auscultation location specific study on the relationship between expiratory-to-inspiratory acoustic patterns and spirometric airflow limitation across age and gender in asthmatic patients
column6: Asthma causes expiratory airflow limitation and is clinically assessed using spirometry, which provides the FEV₁/FVC ratio representing the proportion of air exhaled in the first second relative to total forced vital capacity. Prior studies suggest that respiratory sounds recorded at posterior sites (Left Lower, Left Upper, Right Upper, Right Lower) reflect regional airflow patterns. In this study, we investigate the relationship between the expiratory-to-inspiratory (E/I) spectral power ratio and FEV₁/FVC in 141 participants aged 20-60 years using Spearman correlation across frequency subbands. The 100-200 Hz and 200-400 Hz bands showed significant correlations. Overall, lower posterior sites showed stronger associations; younger adults showed stronger correlations at the Left Lower site, whereas older adults showed stronger correlations at the Left Upper site. Gender-stratified analysis showed stronger Left Lower correlations in males and stronger Left Upper correlations in females.
column7: Dheeraj Harish Kumar(Indian Institute of Science); Sanjana MC(Indian Institute of Science); Perumal Keerthi Priya(Indian Institute of Science); K V Nikhath Khanam(Indian Institute of Science); Uma Maheshwari Krishnaswamy(St. Johns National Academy of Health Sciences); Prasanta Kumar Ghosh(Indian Institute of Science)

column4: Common Cold Corpus: Health-aware robustness study of modern speaker embeddings under physiological domain shift
column6: This study investigates the impact of the common cold on speech using a new ecologically valid corpus. The Common Cold Corpus comprises paired recordings of 85 German speakers, collected remotely via personal devices during acute upper respiratory tract infections and healthy states. Unlike prior lab-based datasets focussing on severe cases, this corpus captures moderate symptoms in everyday acoustic environments. We evaluate eGeMAPS features against modern speaker embeddings (ECAPA2, TitaNet, ReDimNet). While acoustic analysis reveals consistent downward trends in pitch and harmonics-to-noise ratio when ill, only few features survive alpha-error correction. In contrast, speaker embeddings exhibit significant, directed displacement in the identity space under moderate symptomatology. Results suggest that neural models constitute a valuable, more sensitive addition to prosodic analyses, providing a robust foundation for non-invasive digital biomarkers in realistic settings.
column7: Anabell Hacker(Otto von Guericke University; University Hospital Magdeburg); Ingo Siegert(Otto von Guericke University; University Hospital Magdeburg)

column4: Moot-Court: Training-Free Dialectical Reasoning for Depression Detection
column6: Automated depression screening is critical for alleviating medical resource shortages. While Large Language Models (LLMs) advance risk assessment, current methods rely on costly fine-tuning, risking overfitting. To address these challenges, we propose Moot-Court, a training-free reasoning engine inspired by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). By integrating clinical transcripts with textualized acoustic features, Moot-Court prompts a frozen LLM to conduct a simulated court debate, executing dialectical reasoning grounded in clinical symptom networks. Furthermore, we introduce Codex, a dynamic, self-evolving experience library updated via a training-free, reward-based feedback algorithm, explicitly constraining the LLM's reasoning trajectory to suppress hallucinations and enforce accuracy. Experiments on DAIC-WOZ show Moot-Court surpasses fine-tuned models, providing a robust, training-efficient solution.
column7: Yuqing Sun(University of Chinese Academy of Sciences); Jian Zhao(University of Chinese Academy of Sciences); Haoxun Li(University of Chinese Academy of Sciences); Leyuan Qu(University of Chinese Academy of Sciences); Taihao Li(University of Chinese Academy of Sciences)

column4: Who is Speaking or Who is Depressed? A Controlled Study of Speaker Leakage in Speech-Based Depression Detection
column6: This study investigates whether speech-based depression detection models learn depression-related acoustic biomarkers or instead rely on speaker identity cues. Using the DAIC-WOZ dataset, we propose a data-splitting strategy that controls speaker overlap between training and test sets while keeping the training size constant, and evaluate three models of varying complexity. Results show that speaker overlap significantly boosts performance, whereas accuracy drops sharply on unseen speakers. Even with a Domain-Adversarial Neural Network, a substantial performance gap remains. These findings indicate that depression-related features extracted by current speech models are highly entangled with speaker identity. Conventional evaluation protocols may therefore overestimate generalization and clinical utility, highlighting the need for strictly speaker-independent evaluation.
column7: Hsiang-Chen Yeh(Johns Hopkins University); Luqi Sun(Johns Hopkins University); Aurosweta Mahapatra(Johns Hopkins University); Shreeram Suresh Chandra(Johns Hopkins University); Emily Mower Provost(University of Michigan); Berrak Sisman(Johns Hopkins University)

column4: Adapting Self-Supervised Speech Representations for Cross-Lingual Dysarthria Detection in Parkinson's Disease
column6: The limited availability of dysarthric speech data makes cross-lingual detection an important but challenging problem. A key difficulty is that speech representations often encode language-dependent structure that can confound dysarthria detection. We propose a representation-level language shift (LS) that aligns source-language self-supervised speech representations with the target-language distribution using centroid-based vector adaptation estimated from healthy control speech. We evaluate the approach on oral diadochokinesis recordings from Parkinson's disease speech datasets in Czech, German, and Spanish under both cross-lingual and multilingual settings. LS substantially improves sensitivity and F1 in cross-lingual settings, while yielding smaller but consistent gains in multilingual settings. Representation analysis further shows that LS reduces language identity in the embedding space, supporting the interpretation that LS removes language-dependent structure.

column4: Foundational speech models evaluation on multilingual dementia prediction
column6: Dementia is neurological disorder that causes loss of cognitive functions primarily in older adults. Early dementia detection is essential to ensure professional treatment and increase the quality of life of affected people. In this paper, we propose a multilingual approach to the diagnosis of dementia with the use of speech foundational models. We investigate the effectiveness of using acoustic multilingual features for cognitive impairments detection. The work evaluates several popular speech foundational models such as Whisper, WavLM, Hubert, Wav2Vec2 with custom downstream heads. This pipeline is trained in single or multilingual settings and additionally evaluated on unseen languages to test their zero shot capabilities of predicting dementia. This pipeline achieves results of 0.854 F1 score average on combined English datasets and 0.761 F1 score in broader, more challenging multilingual setting.

column4: Who Synthesized This? Joint Deepfake Detection and Generative Source Attribution
column6: We propose a few-shot, open-set framework for joint deepfake detection and generative source attribution. Addressing the rapid evolution of synthetic speech, we introduce a temporal evaluation strategy using the MLAAD v9 dataset, partitioning models by launch year and architectural family. Our model utilizes a WavLM-Large model with targeted LoRA adapters, optimized via-a hierarchical metric learning objective: Conditional AAM Softmax + Center Loss. We simulate real-world forensic deployment by performing prototype-based inference on unseen 2025+ model families, establishing new class centroids with only 12 samples. Evaluated on the ASVspoof 5.0 benchmark, our framework achieves SOTA performance with 0.49% EER and 0.09 minDCF, while attaining 99% accuracy in tracing generated speech to its source. These results demonstrate that hierarchical representation learning and few-shot prototype adaptation provide a robust, scalable defense against the shifting landscape of audio synthesis.
column7: Vishal Kumar(IIIT-Delhi); Vinayak Abrol(IIIT-Delhi); Mathew Magimai Doss(IDIAP Switzerland)

column4: Towards Digital Preservation of Efik: TTS for a Low-Resource African Language
column6: Efik, a tonal language spoken by about 3 million second language speakers and 1.5 million native speakers in Southeastern Nigeria, remains underrepresented in speech synthesis research. We present the first documented end-to-end text-to-speech study for Efik, introducing a curated single speaker corpus of 2,632 utterances totaling three hours and a comparative evaluation of four neural models (VITS, MMS-TTS, SpeechT5, and Orpheus-TTS) under low resource conditions. Native speakers evaluated the systems using MOS, Nat-MOS, and A-MOS. MMS-TTS achieved the highest MOS of 3.80 ± 0.63 and produced more stable long form speech, though tonal errors persisted. Other models showed greater tonal and prosodic inconsistencies. These results provide a reproducible baseline and highlight the need for larger corpora and tone aware modeling for tonal African languages.
column7: Offiong Bassey Edet(University of Cross River State; ML Collective); Emmanuel Oyo-Ita(University of Cross River State); Archibong Okon Archibong(University of Calabar); David Effanga Bassey(University of Calabar); Mbuotidem Sunday Awak(ML Collective)

column4: Rethinking Consent Acquisition for Voice Synthesis: from Static to Dynamic Consent
column6: Voice synthesis raises specific ethical challenges by enabling third parties to generate speech in a person's voice without their involvement or control. Existing safeguards focus on consent acquisition, typically through contractual agreements, and attempt to regulate this practice via standard data-processing models of authorisation. However, voices function not only as data but also as markers of personal identity. As a result, one-time authorisation of voice data, which cannot be de-identified, leaves later uses insufficiently regulated and does not prevent identity-based harms to the original voice sources. This paper critically examines two models of contractual consent acquisition, one general and one specific, to show that neither satisfies the requirements for informed consent. As an alternative, the paper proposes dynamic consent, a type of informed consent that has been used in bioethics, as a governance solution better suited for synthetic voices.
column7: Matilde Nanni(University of Inland Norway)

column4: Ethical and Technical Limits of Deepfake Speech Datasets
column6: Claims about the robustness and fairness of deepfake speech detectors are only as credible as the datasets used to train and evaluate those systems. We present a dataset-level audit of the deepfake speech landscape. We compile and analyze 39 deepfake speech datasets, examining key attributes including accessibility, documentation, demographic and language coverage, dataset scale, and the underlying bona fide speech sources. Our audit reveals two important takeaways. Firstly, fairness assessment is largely infeasible because most datasets lack demographic metadata, and only a few contain gender or language labels. This prevents any meaningful subgroup analysis and leaves other demographic attributes unaddressed. Secondly, we identify substantial overlap in underlying bona fide source corpora across datasets, which can undermine cross-dataset evaluation and lead to overstated generalization claims.
column7: Vojtěch Staněk(Brno University of Technology); Eva Trnovská(Brno University of Technology); Kamil Malinka(Brno University of Technology); Anton Firc(Brno University of Technology)

column4: AI Regulation and the Technical Language of Speech Synthesis
column6: Speech synthesis has garnered increasing interest with global efforts to regulate artificial intelligence (AI), including deepfakes. Policymakers must draft careful wording to prevent societal harm and identify responsible parties. Legal AI provisions must be accurate, especially when instructing responsible parties to act, as seen in the transparency obligations across current AI regulations worldwide. But AI and generative AI are broad terms, and analogies from image and video domains do not translate well to speech. Current AI policy focussing on speech synthesis outputs overlooks portable models and complex workflows wherein speaker embeddings that encode voice identity can be developed independently and later repurposed. This paper traces the convergence of text-to-speech, voice conversion, speaker verification, and speech recognition, highlighting where legal definitions may fail to capture the technical components that enable voice cloning.
column7: Jennifer Williams(University of Southampton)

column4: Tone-Conditioned Curriculum Learning for Low-Resource Bantu Speech Recognition
column6: Southern Bantu languages are spoken by over 80 million people, yet current foundation ASR models still produce zero-shot WER above 100%, which limits practical use in education and public services. We addressed this gap with a tone conditioned curriculum framework for 6 Southern Bantu languages that combined hybrid difficulty scoring, gated adapters driven by tonal statistics and staged curriculum training. We trained on a community corpus and tested transfer to NCHLT to measure robustness beyond matched evaluation. Results revealed clear interactions between architecture and language, with W2V-BERT outperforming Whisper on Nguni languages by 3 to 4 WER points whilst Whisper performed better on Sotho-Tswana languages. W2V-BERT with tone conditioning reached 28.41% average WER across datasets and 23.79% on Xitsonga transfer. No single model suited all 6 languages, so deployment should pair model selection per language with validation across corpora.
column7: Kesego Mokgosi(Technological University Dublin); Vukosi Marivate(University of Pretoria; Lelapa AI); Sitwala Mundia(University of Pretoria); Unarine Netshifhefhe(University of Pretoria); Tsholofelo Mogale(University of Pretoria); Thapelo Sindane(University of Pretoria)

column4: Which Languages Transfer Best to Warlpiri? A Similarity-Based Study for Low-Resource ASR
column6: This paper investigates how language similarity can improve cross-lingual transfer for automatic speech recognition (ASR) in extremely low-resource settings. Warlpiri, an Australian Aboriginal language, has very limited transcribed speech data, making transfer learning essential. We propose a framework combining acoustic similarity from pre-trained speech models with linguistic similarity based on typology, phoneme inventories, grammatical, and syntactic features to rank high-resource source languages and evaluate their effectiveness for ASR transfer to Warlpiri. Experiments with Whisper show that acoustically and typologically similar languages outperform monolingual and multilingual baselines. Assamese and Hindi achieve substantial reductions in word and character error rates. Correlation analysis further indicates that acoustic similarity is the strongest predictor of fine-tuning performance, while phoneme inventory and typological similarity better explain zero-shot transfer.
column7: Pravina Mylvaganam(University of New South Wales); Eliathamby Ambikairajah(University of New South Wales); Ting Dang(University of Melbourne); Vidhyasaharan Sethu(University of New South Wales); Tuende Szalay(University of Sydney)

column4: From Academic Tool to Community Infrastructure: A Call for Indigenous Partnership in Speech Data Governance
column6: We present ELSI (ExELang Legacy Support Interface), a governance platform for managing sensitive child-centered audio datasets that includes recordings from 10 indigenous language communities across multiple continents. While ELSI was designed to balance open science with participant privacy, we identify a fundamental gap: custodianship concentrates control in the hands of European academic researchers, with no formal plan for indigenous communities to govern their own data. We describe the platform, map its current model against CARE and OCAP principles, and issue a concrete call for indigenous community partners to co-design a framework for identifying legitimate community custodians and implementing an enforceable access and control layer. We commit to the architectural and governance changes needed to make this real, and describe what meaningful co-design would look like in practice.
column7: Kaveri K. Sheth(PSL University); Sebastien Christian(UPF, CNRS)

column4: Indigenising Speech Technology: Building a TTS Model for te Reo Māori
column6: This paper introduces an Indigenous-led approach for creating a high-quality text-to-speech (TTS) model for the Māori language (the Indigenous language of Aotearoa, New Zealand). The paper focuses on data curation, collection, and quality assurance, and the decisions made throughout that process, as examples of how this process could be replicated for other Indigenous, endangered, or minority languages. Despite the common assumption that the more data a model has, the better it will perform, this study demonstrates that meticulous attention to detail produces high-quality data and better results for Indigenous languages.
column7: Gianna Leoni(Te Hiku Media); Peter-Lucas Jones(Te Hiku Media); Tūreiti Keith(Te Hiku Media); Suzanne Duncan(Te Hiku Media)

column4: ‘I have to talk proper white ways’: Australian Aboriginal English Speakers’ Experiences with Voice Technologies
column6: This article reports on a qualitative study investigating experiences of Indigenous people in Australia with voice technologies. Many Indigenous people in Australia speak Australian Aboriginal English, a variety which emerged as a result of forced contact between Indigenous communities and English speakers. It is widely used, yet is poorly supported by language technologies. Through Indigenous-led in-depth interviews, this research explores user experiences, attitudes, responses, and challenges encountered while interacting with various speech-enabled devices and applications using Australian Aboriginal English. We find that Indigenous users of ASR-powered technologies report poor experiences with the technologies, which they see as working better for non-Indigenous people. They report switching to speak like white people to get better ASR performance. Our findings reveal significant pressure to speak 'white way' when interacting with technology.
column7: Celeste Rodríguez Louro(University of Western Australia); Glenys Dale Collard(University of Western Australia); Hope Narrier(University of Western Australia); Katrina Cox(University of Western Australia); Lily Hayward(University of Western Australia); Daniel Colbung(University of Western Australia); Ben Hutchinson(Google Australia)

column4: Two-stage semi-supervised learning with pseudo-labels: A case study on Northern Sámi ASR
column6: While Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) has advanced Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), limited labeled data remains a bottleneck for under-resourced languages, and smaller, parameter-efficient models underperform larger counterparts given equal supervised data. We explore semi-supervised learning with SSL models for Northern Sámi, an under-resourced agglutinative language. We compare two approaches: (i) all pseudo-labels generated by a teacher model and (ii) a subset from WER-based multi-teacher agreement. We show that a larger teacher improves out-of-domain generalization of a smaller model by 3.8-33.3% relative CER with no additional labeled data. With comparable data volume, the student benefits as much from pseudo-labels as from human-labeled data. For combining human and pseudo-labeled data, two-stage fine-tuning outperforms single-step mixed training. Overall, we show that lightweight models can approach larger models' performance even after a single pseudo-labeling iteration.
column7: Priyanshi Pal(Aalto University; Instituto Superior Técnico); Yaroslav Getman(Aalto University); Kristiina Ojala(Aalto University); Tamás Grósz(South East Technological University); Mikko Kurimo(Aalto University)

column4: Pashto Common Voice: Building the First Open Speech Corpus for a 60-Million-Speaker Low-Resource Language
column6: We present the Pashto Common Voice corpus — the first large-scale, openly licensed speech resource for Pashto, a language with over 60 million native speakers largely absent from open speech technology. Through a community effort spanning 2022-2025, the corpus grew from 1.5 hours and 5 contributors to 147 total hours and 1,483 unique speakers across ten Mozilla Common Voice releases (CV14-CV23). Speaker participation increased approximately 108-fold between CV17 and CV18, coinciding with a VOA Pashto broadcast campaign. We describe the full methodology: interface localisation, Wikipedia-based sentence extraction with automated filtering, phonemically targeted contributions for the four most frequently dropped Pashto characters, and multi-channel community outreach. MCV23 contains 107,781 clips (60,337 validated; 82.33 validated hours) across 13 content domains. Fine-tuning Whisper Base on the MCV20 yields 13.4% WER on the MCV20 test split, against the published Whisper Base zero-shot WER of 99.0% on Pashto.
column7: Hanif Rahman(Pashto DAO); Shafeeq ur Rehman(Pashto DAO)

column4: Amadea: An AI Companion for Pitch-Aware Spoken Language Practice
column6: We present Amadea: an interactive speech learning platform for pitch-sensitive languages, including pitch accent languages such as Japanese and lexical tonal languages such as Mandarin. The system pairs an AI companion interface with real-time pronunciation feedback. When a learner speaks, the system transcribes the input and generates a native reference equivalent audio of the phrase. The system aligns the two audio files and compares their normalised fundamental-frequency (F0) contours to produce a pitch-pattern score. A graph visualising any pitch divergence throughout the phrase is then presented to the user. Amadea supports structured lessons as well as open-ended companion dialogue, with real-time feedback on both.
column7: Mrigendra Agrawal(The University of Queensland; Amadea); Ryan Tsui(Amadea; University of Edinburgh); Kyaw Maung Maung Tet Toe(Amadea)

column4: Real-Time CARFAC/SAI-derived Pitchogram for Seeing and Correcting Pronunciation in Mandarin Chinese Tones
column6: We present a Computer-Assisted Pronunciation Training (CAPT) system that incorporates a CARFAC (Cascade of Asymmetric Resonators with Fast-Acting Compression) and SAI (Stabilised Auditory Image)-derived pitchogram as an alternative to conventional spectrogram-based visualisation, which often fails to clearly represent temporal fine structure. The system features a dual-screen interface that provides real-time pitchogram feedback alongside reference pitchograms generated using Google Text-to-Speech. This design enables learners to perceive and produce the four Mandarin tones by comparing their speech with reference patterns. Our approach highlights the potential of pitchogram-based visualisation to support intuitive, real-time pronunciation practice for second language (L2) learners.
column7: Yuka Maruyama(University of New South Wales); Jason Orlosky(Augusta University); Chris Lee(Georgia Institute of Technology); Flora Salim(University of New South Wales); Thad Starner(Georgia Institute Technology); Benjamin Tag(University of New South Wales)

column4: AURORA: A Web-based Authoring System for Bridging Aural-Oral Language Training and Communicative Practice
column6: AURORA is a web-based authoring system for designing and deploying aural-oral training and communicative practice. For aural training, shadowing and its variants were implemented, and listening disfluency (LD) was measured and visualized. For oral training, imitative overlapping and its variants were used to quantify pronunciation deviations (PD) in learners' speech. For communicative practice, learners engaged in task-based oral conversations with ChatGPT, followed by prompt-based automatic assessment. With AURORA, two-month, inter-semester courseware was provided, where learners practiced for about 30 minutes per day to improve their listening, speaking, and communicative skills. This courseware supported university students during the transition to English-medium instruction, as more courses are offered in English. Training outcomes were evaluated objectively using LD and PD and subjectively through questionnaires. A tutorial workshop on AURORA was held for teachers in February.
column7: Nobuaki Minematsu(The University of Tokyo)

column4: VoxKit: Desktop Phone Alignment and Goodness of Pronunciation Analysis
column6: VoxKit is an extensible desktop workbench that addresses a gap in available tools: no desktop application integrates forced alignment and goodness of pronunciation analysis in a single pipeline, creating a barrier to adoption for speech researchers working with clinical populations. With VoxKit, researchers can register datasets, select and train alignment engines, generate and compare alignments, and compute phone-level goodness of pronunciation scores within a single interface.
column7: Nina R Benway(University of Maryland - College Park); Beckett Frey(University of Wisconsin - Madison); Tristan Mahr(University of Wisconsin - Madison); Michael McAuliffe(University of Wisconsin - Madison); Prad Kadambi(Arizona State University); Visar Berisha(Arizona State University); Katherine Hustad(University of Wisconsin - Madison)

column4: AdaptLingo: A Speech-to-Speech English Practice System with Fluency-Adaptive Responses
column6: We demonstrate AdaptLingo, an open-source, speech-to-speech English conversational agent for second-language learners. Beginners may be overwhelmed by many static language learning systems, which use complex language and fast speech, while advanced learners may disengage from simplified dialogue. AdaptLingo addresses this problem by predicting a learner's spoken fluency from temporal acoustic features, constraining responses to the learner's EIKEN-aligned vocabulary level, and adapting text-to-speech rate. In demonstration, users speak to the chatbot and receive spoken responses adapted to beginner, intermediate, or advanced fluency. Preliminary evaluation shows fluency classification works well on labeled data but remains challenging on noisy user-study speech, and user feedback suggests that adaptive spoken practice is promising when matched to learner background and conversational goals.
column7: Zackary Rackauckas(Columbia University)

column4: lisero: An interactive practice app for learning Romanian Sign Language
column6: Romanian Sign Language (LSR) was officially recognized in 2020, yet it remains severely under-resourced and insufficiently supported in educational contexts, including special education. Accessible and interactive learning tools are limited. We present, lisero, a freely accessible mobile app designed to support learning LSR through structured lessons and interactive exercises. Originally developed to support infant-caregiver interactions and support bimodal bilingualism, the app has been extended to cover general LSR learning scenarios. lisero features lesson-based content, practice exercises, and a growing sign dictionary. Gamification elements, as well as options to save and share signs, aim to enhance user engagement and community participation. The system is designed for both hearing users and deaf and hard-of hearing learners.
column7: Anisia Popescu(Université Paris 8; Fundatia CODA); Serban Din(Solid Technologies; Fundatia CODA); Marinela Axinte(Universitatea Babeş-Bolyai; Fundatia CODA)

column4: SayCheck: Gamified Speech Practice and Attribute-Based Speech Analysis for Children
column6: This paper presents SayCheck, an AI-powered speech therapy platform designed to support children's speech practice through engaging gameplay and automated speech analysis. The platform combines two integrated components: Say Bananas, a Mario-style speech therapy game that motivates home practice, and PhoneAid, an automatic speech analysis system that evaluates children's speech productions at both the phoneme and phonological attribute levels. The system enables therapists and caregivers to configure targeted speech exercises while providing detailed diagnostic feedback about pronunciation performance. PhoneAid extends traditional phoneme-level assessment by analysing articulatory and phonological speech attributes, allowing more informative feedback about how speech sounds differ from target productions. A demonstration of the system highlights the workflow from gameplay-based speech elicitation to detailed automatic speech assessment and summary reporting.
column7: Mostafa Shahin(University of New South Wales); Kirrie Ballard(University of Sydney); Beena Ahmed(University of New South Wales)

column4: A Speech-First Character Interface for Stylized Japanese Dialogue Practice
column6: We present Jouzu, a mobile Show & Tell demonstration of expressive persona-conditioned spoken interaction for Japanese language practice. In Jouzu, attendees choose a fictional character, type or speak a prompt, hear a character-specific Style-BERT-VITS2 voice response, compare how multiple personas realize the same utterance through wording, register, and speech, and tap unfamiliar Japanese words for in-place reading support. The demo foregrounds speech as the primary medium for experiencing persona, affect, and learner feedback, rather than treating audio as an add-on to a text chatbot. This paper describes the runnable interaction loop, persona-conditioned generation, expressive TTS pipeline, speech-input path, comparison mode, and booth workflow that combine LLM dialogue, character voice synthesis, and vocabulary scaffolding in a live Japanese-practice system.
column7: Zackary Rackauckas(RoleGaku)

column4: CodeVaani: A Multilingual, Voice-Based Code Learning Assistant
column6: Programming education often assumes English proficiency and text-based interaction, creating barriers for students in non-English speaking countries like India. We present CodeVaani, a multilingual voice-enabled code assistant built into IIT Bombay’s Learning Management System, helping learners explore programming concepts in their native languages. The system integrates Indic ASR, a code-aware transcription refinement, and a code model to generate responses in both text and audio. In a study with 28 beginner programmers, over 89% rated the experience as fair or above. CodeVaani offers on-demand, scalable, multilingual support, lowering the entry barrier for students with limited English proficiency and demonstrating how voice-based AI can make programming education more inclusive. Supplementary artefacts and demo video are available.
column7: Jayant Havare(Indian Institute of Technology Bombay); Srikanth Tamilselvam(IBM Research India); Ashish Mittal(Google DeepMind India); Shalaka Thorat(Indian Institute of Technology Bombay); Soham Jadia(Indian Institute of Technology Bombay); Varsha Apte(Indian Institute of Technology Bombay); Ganesh Ramakrishnan(Indian Institute of Technology Bombay)

column4: Auditory Contrast Network for Text-Free Prominence Detection
column6: We introduce the Auditory Contrast Network (ACN), a model with up to 238 trainable parameters that encodes three psychoacoustic principles - pairwise contrast, cue independence, and forward dominance - into an interpretable detector of word-level perceived prominence. Using only three acoustic features and no text, ACN achieves r = 0.412 on cross-corpus transfer (Helsinki Prosody → Emphases), matching a frozen 94.6M-parameter wav2vec2 baseline (r = 0.409) at 120× lower latency; adding text features raises r to 0.451. The learned weights suggest forward-dominant context use (over 96% preceding across all cues), strict locality (±1 word), and the cue hierarchy duration > energy > spectral ≫ F0, consistent with established findings while preserving a direct architectural readout. The acoustic-only result makes ACN suitable for on-device applications where text is unavailable, such as hearing aids and real-time pronunciation monitoring.
column7: Kosuke Shimizu(University of Tsukuba); Keiichi Zempo(University of Tsukuba)

column4: F0 realization of prosodic focus across adulthood in Jianghuai Mandarin
column6: This study examined age-related variation in the F0 realization of prosodic focus across adulthood in Jianghuai Mandarin. A focus production task was conducted with young, middle-aged, and older adult speakers, who produced sentences with neutral focus and three types of narrow focus. The results show that Jianghuai Mandarin exhibits the canonical tri-zone F0 pattern, reflected in both mean F0 and F0 excursion, and that this global pattern is largely preserved across age groups. However, fine-grained F0 adjustments, i.e., the contrast between narrow and neutral focus, show age-related variation. In particular, older speakers demonstrate greater post-focus compression in mean F0 compared with young and middle-aged speakers. These findings indicate that prosodic focus across adulthood is characterized by stable global F0 patterning but age-sensitive fine-grained F0 adjustment.
column7: Xinxian Zhao(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Xiaohu Yang(Tongji University)

column4: Prosodic Realization of Focus in Yi-Mandarin Bilingual Speakers: On-Focus Expansion without Post-Focus Compression
column6: Post-focus compression (PFC) is absent in Yi (Nuosu), a Tibeto-Burman tone language, but present in Beijing Mandarin. We examined whether Yi-Mandarin bilingual speakers produce PFC in L2 Mandarin, using delta-F0 and intensity as primary measures and duration as a secondary measure, across initial, medial, and final focus conditions. Yi speakers produced on-focus F0 expansion fully comparable to Beijing controls, yet showed no post-focus compression across all conditions in both F0 and intensity. Individual variation in Mandarin language background did not predict post-focus F0 among Yi speakers. These results demonstrate a complete dissociation between intact on-focus expansion and absent post-focus compression, suggesting that when the L1 entirely lacks PFC, the mechanism may be suppressed in L2 production even under prolonged bilingual contact-consistent with the view that on-focus expansion and post-focus compression constitute functionally independent prosodic modules with distinct acquisition trajectories.
column7: Ziyu Zhang(Flinders University); Chenyu Li(Johns Hopkins University)

column4: The (non-)universality of prominence and Intonation Phrases: German and Hungarian listeners' perception of an unfamiliar language
column6: This study adopts a typological perspective to examine the nonuniversality of acoustic cues used to perceive prosodic prominence and Intonation Phrase (IP) boundaries. By using speech extracts from an unfamiliar language, we analyse the role of acoustic cues beyond the lexical and pragmatic factors. Employing Rapid Prosody Transcription, we presented speech extracts from Urdu to German and Hungarian listeners who were asked to identify prominent words and IP boundaries. We found that listener groups relied on different F0 contours and scaling patterns to perceive prominence. Moreover, they exhibited variable inter- and intra-rater agreement when identifying IP boundaries. By presenting the same Urdu stimuli to listeners of typologically diverse languages, we offer a nuanced perspective to investigate within- and between-group (dis)agreement. This sheds light on language-specific and cross-linguistic variability in the perception of prosodic phenomena.
column7: Farhat Jabeen(Bielefeld University); Ákos Buza(Bielefeld University); Ella Reimann(Bielefeld University)

column4: Broad Focus Rise(-fall) Declaratives in Venetan: Investigating Typological Outliers in Italo-Romance Intonation
column6: Intonational rises in unmarked declaratives are cross-linguistically rare. While reported for Venetan (an Italo-Romance variety spoken in north-eastern Italy), little is known about their properties, or indeed Venetan intonation in general. To address this, we investigate the prevalence, distribution and properties of intonational rise(-falls) in broad focus declaratives in gambellarese, a central-western Venetan dialect, for semi-spontaneous speech. We find rise(-falls) to be roughly as common as falls, and to occur regardless of position of lexical stress, strongly indicating the existence of an alternative unmarked rising nuclear tune for declaratives, distinct from the H+L* L% tune reported for Italian and other Italo-Romance varieties. We also examine the phonetic effects of word-final stress (common in Venetan) on tonal alignment with regard to these rise(-falls).
column7: Elinor Payne(University of Oxford); Angelo Dian(University of Oxford)

column4: Should Robots Sound more like Machines than like Humans? User Expectations Affect the Perception of Prosody in TTS Voices
column6: Prosodic and indexical features of artificial voices, like naturalness, tone, and emotion, are often treated as distinct from intelligibility. Yet prosody can be critical: Consider, "She has to pull Bart" (without commas/prosodic boundaries) versus "She has to pull, Bart" (with commas/prosodic boundaries). Here, we asked how humans disambiguated such sentences while listening to a robot avatar, as prosodic and indexical features in the robot voice were manipulated. Prosodic pitch changes to make the voice either affective or monotonic had little effect on intelligibility. Surprisingly, indexical changes to increase machine-like (and less human-like) voice quality, despite being phonetically irrelevant to this prosodic contrast, increased intelligibility, but only for sentences with commas. Results imply that hearing machine-like voices changes listener expectations, biasing or pushing listeners to hear prosodic boundaries (i.e., commas) that are otherwise hard to detect.
column7: Ha Eun Shim(Simon Fraser University; University of Massachusetts Amherst); Paige Tuttösí(Simon Fraser University; Enchanted Tools); Olivia Yung(Simon Fraser University); Ivan Fong(Simon Fraser University); Sara Ng(Simon Fraser University); Angelica Lim(Simon Fraser University); Yue Wang(Simon Fraser University); H. Henny Yeung(Simon Fraser University; CNRS & Université Paris Cité)

column4: WeSep: A Modular and Cue-Composable Framework for Target Speaker Extraction
column6: The study of Target Speaker Extraction (TSE) aims to isolate a desired speaker from overlapping speech mixture given auxiliary cues. Existing systems are typically designed for specific cue types, limiting flexibility when cue availability varies across scenarios. We present WeSep, a unified framework that reformulates TSE as a heterogeneous cue-conditioned learning problem. In WeSep, cue modules and separator backbones are decoupled through standardized interfaces, enabling configurable cue injection and flexible integration of diverse modalities. The design enables systematic study of cue structure, intra-and cross-modal interaction, and dynamic cue availability within a shared optimization framework, facilitating adaptation to real-world conditions. Experiments across enrollment, spatial, visual, and textual cues reveal modality-dependent characteristics and demonstrate stable optimization under heterogeneous cue availability. The toolkit is publicly available.

column4: TF-MoE: Time-Frequency Mixture-of-Experts for Efficient Speech Separation
column6: Recent advances in speech separation (SS) have led to compact front-end models with small parameter sizes, yet their high computational cost remains a major barrier for deployment on edge devices. To address this, we propose TF-MoE, a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) framework that enhances model capacity with almost no increase in inference cost. Our method introduces dynamic expert specialization in time and frequency dimensions through alternating time-wise and frequency-wise MoE modules, each dynamically selecting experts per frame or mel band. Built upon a mel-band-splitting Conformer backbone, TF-MoE achieves strong performance on SS tasks under low-compute settings. Experimental results demonstrate that TF-MoE consistently improves separation performance under computation cost constraints, outperforming BSRNN by +3.8 dB SDR on Libri2Mix with comparable 4.1 GMACs/s inference cost. This positions TF-MoE as a promising candidate for edge-device deployment.
column7: Qinzhe Hu(Shanghai Jiaotong University); Chenda Li(Shanghai Jiaotong University); Wangyou Zhang(Shanghai Jiaotong University); Shujie Liu(Microsoft Research Asia); Yan Lu(Microsoft Research Asia); Yanmin Qian(Shanghai Jiaotong University)

column4: Sweep-RSE: Streaming Region-of-Interest Speech Extraction in Multi-Talker Scenarios via Explicit Spatial Sweeping
column6: Region-of-Interest (ROI) speech extraction is crucial for AR/VR and hearing aids but challenging in streaming multi-talker scenarios. Existing methods rely on implicit boundary conditioning, often failing to isolate targets under dense interference or suppress noise in empty regions. We propose Sweep-RSE, a lightweight, fully causal framework utilizing an explicit Align & Sweep mechanism. By actively scanning the ROI, our model locks onto target signals via phase coherency and explicitly models spatial discrepancies to reject outliers. Integrated with a Region Speech Detector, it ensures real-time O(1) processing. Experiments demonstrate Sweep-RSE achieves precise target extraction in complex scenarios and effectively suppresses false alarms in silent regions, operating efficiently with only 1.66M parameters and 3.05 GMACs.
column7: Hogeon Yu(Hyundai Motor Company); SeongHun Noh(Hyundai Motor Company); Hyunsik Choi(Hyundai Motor Company); Sihyun Joo(Hyundai Motor Company)

column4: Online Audiovisual Speaker Separation Using Efficient Visual Knowledge Distillation
column6: We present an efficient visual knowledge distillation (VKD) strategy to address the causal audiovisual speaker separation (AVSS) problem. Causal AVSS systems suffer from significant performance degradation due to the absence of the future context and the reliance on heavily parameterized visual embedding models originally developed non-causally. VKD progressively transfers knowledge from a causally inferred pre-trained visual front-end to a lightweight, task-oriented student model via a dynamic weighting mechanism, preserving speaker-discriminative embeddings while reducing overall system complexity. VKD compresses the visual front-end by more than 48 times in model size and 7.5 times in computational complexity. Through extensive comparisons, evaluations, and ablation studies on multiple datasets, we demonstrate that VKD combined with a top-performing online AVSS separator achieves the state-of-the-art causal AVSS performance.

column4: DTT-BSR+: A Generative-Regression Cascade for Music Source Restoration
column6: Music source restoration (MSR) requires jointly addressing source unmixing and the inversion of non-linear production effects. Current methods struggle to achieve accurate target signal reconstruction while maintaining semantic consistency. To address this limitation, we propose DTT-BSR+, a two-stage cascade MSR system that decouples distribution fitting from signal reconstruction into separate stages. A generative DTT-BSR separator in the first stage produces stems matching the prior of clean sources, and a modified Demucs network in the second stage enhances the first stage output using time-domain and multi-resolution spectral losses. DTT-BSR+ improves multi-mel signal-to-noise ratio (MMSNR) over the single-stage DTT-BSR across all stems, and surpasses the state-of-the-art X-LANCE MSR system on five stems. We also reveal through Fréchet Audio Distance (FAD) decomposition an implicit trade-off between signal reconstruction accuracy and semantic distribution fitting across stems.
column7: Youran Ni(Wuhan University); Shihong Tan(Wuhan University); Yuzhu Wang(Tampere University); Gongping Huang(Wuhan University)

column4: Adaptive Hard-Pair Sampling via Curriculum Learning for Speech Separation
column6: End-to-end neural speech separation systems have achieved strong average scale-invariant signal-to-distortion ratio (SI-SDR) scores, yet still struggle with mixtures where speakers have highly similar timbre. These difficult cases reduce robustness and raise concerns about real-world generalization. To address this, we propose a curriculum hard-pair sampling strategy. During training, a pairwise speaker-speaker difficulty matrix is built and updated online based on the SI-SDR score of separating each speaker pair. Each mixture for model training is constructed by first randomly sampling an anchor speaker, and the interference speaker is sampled based on a temperature-controlled Softmax which gives more weights to speakers that are, as indicated by the difficulty matrix, difficult to be separated with the anchor speaker. Results on Libri2Mix show that the proposed method consistently improves performance, especially for similar-timbre mixtures, without additional training overhead.
column7: Pengjie Shen(Inner Mongolia University; Southern University of Science and Technology); Xueliang Zhang(Inner Mongolia University); Zhong-Qiu Wang(Southern University of Science and Technology)
