column4: AURA: Audio-Geometry Conditioned U-Net Refinement with Flow Matching for High-Fidelity Monaural-to-Binaural Synthesis
column6: Spatial audio is crucial for immersive listening, and binaural rendering is particularly appealing due to its alignment with human auditory perception. However, synthesizing high-quality binaural audio from monaural input remains challenging, as spatial cues must be inferred while preserving both spatial realism and fine-grained timbral detail, limiting its use in VR/AR and telepresence. To address this issue, we propose AURA, a two-stage binaural synthesis framework that explicitly models the relationship between monaural audio and source direction. The first stage combines global context modeling and local texture extraction to produce a coarse binaural estimate. The second stage refines this estimate with a generative mechanism, enhancing spatial cues and spectral details for high-fidelity output. Extensive experiments show that AURA outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both subjective evaluations and objective metrics (Wave-L2: 0.123 vs. 0.128).
column7: Wenjie Zhang(Harbin Institute of Technology(Shenzhen)); Changjun He(Harbin Institute of Technology(Shenzhen)); Yinghan Cao(Harbin Institute of Technology(Shenzhen)); Shiyun Xu(Harbin Institute of Technology(Shenzhen)); Mingjiang Wang(Harbin Institute of Technology(Shenzhen))

column4: GISNO: Neural Operator-based HRTF Personalization from 3D Meshes via Differentiable Helmholtz Rendering
column6: Individualized head-related transfer functions (HRTFs) are crucial for immersive audio, yet their acquisition remains challenging. Existing deep-learning approaches are often constrained by discrete sampling grids and lose fine morphological details during mesh preprocessing. In this work, we propose a geometrically informed spherical neural operator (GISNO), a framework that reformulates HRTF prediction as a continuous operator-learning problem. By integrating a discretization-invariant neural operator with a differentiable Helmholtz-integral renderer, our model learns to map 3D head geometry to continuous boundary pressure fields. Experiments on the HUTUBS dataset demonstrate that our method outperforms representative baselines in log-spectral distortion. Furthermore, the physics-integrated architecture enables multi-dimensional zero-shot generalization across unseen spatial densities, distances, and frequencies, offering a robust solution for scalable HRTF personalization.
column7: Chen Huang(Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Lei Zhou(Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Hongqing Liu(Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Lu Gan(Brunel University); Liming Shi(Chongqing University of Posts and Telecommunications)

column4: TTBA: Spatial Prompted Text to Binaural Audio Generation Using Transformer
column6: Binaural audio can deliver an immersive listening experience, and it is valuable for virtual reality, gaming, and creative content production. While recent text-to-audio models can generate high-fidelity audio, they still struggle to generate binaural signals with directional control and accurate spatial perception. To address this issue, we propose TTBA, a text-to-binaural audio generation model. TTBA combines a cross-arranged discrete representation with a transformer-based autoregressive backbone to jointly model semantic content and spatial cues. We further design a spatial prompt encoder that maps explicit spatial prompts into a conditioning representation, which is fused with text features to guide binaural token generation. We use a monaural generation model as guidance and emphasize both content accuracy and inter-channel discrepancy. Experiments on the BEWO-1M dataset show that TTBA can generate binaural audio with spatial awareness and controllable directionality.
column7: Changjun He(Harbin Institute of Technology); Lianyu Zhou(Harbin Institute of Technology); Yukun Qian(Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen)); Shiyun Xu(Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen)); Wenjie Zhang(Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen)); Mingjiang Wang(Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen)); Weiping Chen(Harbin Institute of Technology)

column4: Spec2Spatial: A Time-Frequency Spatial Attention Network for Binaural Audio Synthesis
column6: Binaural audio can provide realism and immersion, and it is widely used in scenarios such as virtual reality. The difficulty of binaural recording has motivated research on binaural audio synthesis. Deep learning-based binaural synthesis is promising, but existing methods still perform poorly, especially in reproducing interaural differences. In this paper, we propose Spec2Spatial, a time-frequency spatial attention network for binaural audio synthesis. Specifically, we introduce an interaural spatial attention network to capture left-right relations in the frequency domain. Additionally, we propose a condition fusion residual network that uses sound source position to adjust time-frequency features. Experiments on the Binaural Speech dataset show that Spec2Spatial synthesizes realistic binaural audio, achieving state-of-the-art DILD (1.250), DITD (0.034), and MRSTFT (1.174).
column7: Changjun He(Harbin Institute of Technology); Wenjie Zhang(Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen)); Shiyun Xu(Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen)); Lianyu Zhou(Harbin Institute of Technology); Weiping Chen(Harbin Institute of Technology); Mingjiang Wang(Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen))

column4: Geometry-Informed Distributed Acoustic Scene Understanding
column6: Acoustic scene understanding in multi-room environments is a difficult task. Most existing systems use a single centralized microphone array, and they often fail because walls and doors block sound signals. To address this challenge, we propose a geometry-informed distributed acoustic scene understanding framework. Our system leverages distributed microphones and uses an audio spectrogram transformer and a topology-aware graph neural network to fuse spatio-temporal acoustic features. Then, these features are decoded into discrete semantic triplets. Finally, a frozen large language model combines these symbolic observations with the environmental geometry. This allows the system to perform spatial understanding, infer plausible missing transitions, and generate a physically consistent narrative of the scene. Experiments on a custom multi-room simulator demonstrate that our framework outperforms centralized baselines and improves spatial consistency under simulated occlusion.
column7: Yiyuan Yang(University of Oxford); Shitong Xu(University of Oxford); Niki Trigoni(University of Oxford); Andrew Markham(University of Oxford)

column4: Branch-wise Complementary Attention for Acoustic Scene Classification
column6: Acoustic scene classification (ASC) requires lightweight models that effectively capture diverse temporal and spectral cues for mobile devices. Multi-branch convolutional architectures improve receptive field diversity, but their outputs are typically aggregated without explicitly modeling complementary relationships or compensating for branch-specific limitations. We propose a branch-wise complementary attention (BCA) module that allocates channel, time, frequency, and joint time-frequency attention maps across branches according to their receptive field characteristics. By explicitly addressing the inherent limitations of each branch, BCA enhances multi-scale feature integration beyond simple aggregation. Integrated into the Rep-Mobile backbone, BCA consistently outperforms existing attention mechanisms on the TAU Urban Acoustic Scenes 2020 and 2022 Mobile benchmarks.
column7: Seung-Gyu Han(Hanyang University); Jinwoo Jung(Hanyang University); Pil Moo Byun(Hanyang University); Won-Gook Choi(Hanyang University); Joon-Hyuk Chang(Hanyang University, Seoul, Republic of Korea)

column4: CoSTALA: Compositional Spatio-Temporal Audio-Language Alignment via Multi-Grain Hierarchical Contrastive Learning
column6: Conventional audio language models (ALMs) have made significant progress in achieving alignment between auditory and textual representations, including recent explorations in spatial audio. However, in daily spatial scenarios, they still cannot effectively process multi-event audio sequences. Current approaches primarily rely on coarse-grained contrastive learning with global auditory and textual features, lacking the resolution to distinguish multiple sequential events. To overcome these limitations, we propose CoSTALA—a novel training paradigm that transitions from purely global alignment to fine-grained spatio-temporal reasoning. By constructing a multi-granularity hierarchical loss function system, we achieve explicit modeling of temporal dependencies, and successfully anchors individual acoustic events to preserve their semantic purity. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CoSTALA significantly establish a powerful new framework for spatio-temporal audio understanding.
column7: Peiwei Ren(Xi’an Jiaotong Liverpool University); Jinbo Hu(Xiaomi Inc.); Fang Kang(University of Oulu); Shan Liang(Xi’an Jiaotong Liverpool University); Yin Cao(Chinese Academy of Sciences)

column4: Perceptually Weighted Minimum Mean Square Error Precoding for Acoustic Multi-User MIMO in Vehicular Personal Sound Zones
column6: To address multiuser interference in in-vehicle personal sound zones (PSZ), this paper proposes a perceptually weighted acoustic multi-user MIMO (MU-MIMO) precoding framework. Traditional spatial audio methods often neglect human psychoacoustics, treating cross-talk merely as uniform physical energy. To overcome this, we integrate a psychoacoustic masking model into the Weighted Minimum Mean Square Error (WMMSE) criterion. The algorithm dynamically assigns stronger distortion penalties to perceptually sensitive time-frequency regions while relaxing constraints in zones heavily masked by target speech. By actively coordinating precoding filters, this method minimizes the perceptually weighted MSE, jointly balancing inter-user interference and target-signal distortion. Validated using measured impulse responses from a real car cabin, the approach shows improvements in objective speech quality over baselines, offering a scalable solution for smart cockpit audio.
column7: Huihui Wei( Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Dengke Deng(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Pengcheng Luo(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Weiyu You(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Xiaojuan Zhang(Institute of Advanced Intelligence and Computing); Genke Yang(Shanghai Jiao Tong University)

column4: SA-HRTF: A Sound-Assisted Approach to Personalized HRTF Modeling
column6: Head-related transfer functions (HRTFs) are essential for immersive binaural audio rendering, whereas generic HRTFs are often inadequate for accurately reproducing individual spatial cues. Although neural-network-based personalized HRTF modeling has progressed rapidly, accurate reconstruction under sparse measurements remains challenging because limited spatial information hinders reliable estimation. To address this issue, we propose a sound-assisted HRTF (SA-HRTF) model that incorporates binaural acoustic information into personalized HRTF estimation. The proposed architecture adopts a dual-branch design: the primary branch exploits structural features from an existing database to generate an initial estimate, while the auxiliary branch extracts perceptual cues from sound signals to provide supplementary predictions. A fusion module combines the outputs of the two branches to produce a more accurate personalized HRTF. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
column7: Qingyin Zhao(Inner Mongolia University); Siyuan Chen(Inner Mongolia University); De Hu(Inner Mongolia University)

column4: Bayesian Model-Based Assessment of Spatial and Source Priors in Sagittal-Plane Sound Localization
column6: Sagittal-plane localization in the polar dimension is ill-posed, entangling unknown source spectra and head-related transfer functions. Humans may resolve this ambiguity through sensory evidence and learned priors. We evaluated these priors using a Bayesian observer with an ecological source prior and five spatial priors. Models were calibrated against human responses across cochlear implant (CI)-like reductions in spectral resolution. Across conditions, the models captured the decrease in polar and quadrant errors as spectral resolution improved. The ecological source prior provided limited additional benefit within the present model implementation, whereas predictions were more sensitive to spatial-prior configuration. No single spatial prior was consistently preferred, although asymmetric variants showed better overall agreement with human data. These findings support individualized modeling of spatial hearing under reduced spectral resolution.
column7: Yunda Chen(Shenzhen University); Nengheng Zheng(Shenzhen University)

column4: ARCHES: An Agent-Based Refinement Cycle for Hierarchical Synthesis of Sound Effects for Variety Shows
column6: Sound effects for variety shows can greatly improve viewer engagement, which currently relies on a manual process. This approach is heavily dependent on the experience of human editors. While recent advancements in audio generation methods have shown promising performance, they struggle to meet the unique demands of variety shows. The past methods exhibit critical limitations in temporal precision, content diversity, and contextual understanding. To overcome these limitations, we propose ARCHES (Agent-based Refinement Cycle for HiErarchical Synthesis), a novel framework that leverages multi-agent collaboration and retrieval-augmented generation to automatically produce high-quality, contextually appropriate sound effects. The framework contains an iterative workflow of planning, generation, and refinement. The core components of this framework are three modules: the Auditory Unified Retrieval Augmentation (AURA) module for content diversity, the Adaptive eXpert Intelligent Switch (AXIS) module for specific fine-grained refinement, and a Creative Experience Bank (CEB) which allows the system to learn from past generation process. To validate our approach, we constructed the first large-scale, fine-grained dataset for this task, the Variety Show Sound Effect Benchmark (VSSE-Bench). Extensive experiments demonstrate that ARCHES significantly outperforms state-of-the-art (SOTA) on both objective and subjective metrics. The demos are anonymously available at https://arches-bench.github.io/.
column7: Wentao Lei(The Hongkong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou); Li Liu(The Hongkong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou))

column4: Scalable Direction-Following TTS via Voice Impression-Guided Pseudo Triplet Construction
column6: Voice actors often re-read the same script while modifying their delivery in response to performance directions. We study this setting as direction-following TTS, where a system generates a new utterance that reflects a given direction relative to a reference utterance while preserving speaker identity and linguistic content. A key challenge is the lack of training data capturing such relative modifications. To address this, we propose a scalable pseudo-triplet construction pipeline that generates (reference utterance, direction text, modified utterance) triplets. It generates controlled style variations using an impression-controllable TTS model and uses an LLM to produce natural language directions from estimated impression differences. Experimental results demonstrate that pseudo-triplets alone enable stable speaker-preserving modification, and that combining pseudo and recorded data further improves direction alignment while maintaining speaker similarity.
column7: Kenichi Fujita(NTT); Yusuke Ijima(NTT)

column4: Poly-InstructTTS: Learning In-the-Wild Expressive Speech Synthesis from Open-Ended Instructions
column6: While recent text-to-speech (TTS) models achieve high naturalness, controlling fine-grained expression via natural-language instructions remains challenging. We introduce Poly-InstructTTS, which learns expressive speech from open-ended instructions using in-the-wild audiovisual data. We build a scalable multi-modal pipeline to construct a 1,000-hour instruction-annotated corpus covering 1,000+ fine-grained emotions and styles. The framework uses a prompt-free GPT with attribute-based thinking tokens, followed by a flow-matching module that injects timbre from a reference audio. We also present a speaker fine-tuning procedure to transfer instruction control to specific speakers while preserving persona. We further extend InstructTTSEval with broader tasks. Experiments show that Poly-InstructTTS delivers strong performance in instruction adherence and expressiveness. Audio demos and the expanded testset are available on our project page.
column7: Junhui Zhang(ZuoYeBang Technology); Qianhui Xu(ZuoYeBang Technology); Qingxiang Guo(ZuoYeBang Technology); Dawei Yang(ZuoYeBang Technology); Ling Miao(ZuoYeBang Technology); Qiangqiang Wang(ZuoYeBang Technology); Yang Song(ZuoYeBang Technology)

column4: Spiking Vocos: An Energy-Efficient Neural Vocoder
column6: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs), widely recognized for their high energy efficiency due to their event-driven nature, offer a promising solution for low-resource scenarios. In this paper, we propose Spiking Vocos, a novel spiking neural vocoder with ultra-low energy consumption. To mitigate the inherent information bottleneck in SNNs, we design a Spiking ConvNeXt module to reduce Multiply-Accumulate (MAC) operations and incorporate an amplitude shortcut path to preserve crucial signal dynamics. Furthermore, to bridge the performance gap with its Artificial Neural Network (ANN) counterpart, we introduce a self-architectural distillation strategy to effectively transfer knowledge. A lightweight Temporal Shift Module is also integrated to enhance the model's ability to fuse information across the temporal dimension. Experiments demonstrate that our model achieves performance comparable to its ANN counterpart with only 14.7% of the energy. The source code and demos are available at https://github.com/pymaste r17/Spiking-Vocos.
column7: Yukun Chen(Xi'an Jiaotong University); Zhaoxi Mu(Xi'an Jiaotong University); Andong Li(Chinese Academy of Sciences); Peilin Li(Xi'an Jiaotong University); Xingyu Yang(Xi'an Jiaotong University)

column4: Stabilizing Instruction Supervision for Instruct-TTS via Controllable Diversification and Drift Filtering
column6: Instruct-TTS systems expand structured style labels into natural-language training instructions through LLM rewriting, yet we find that over 40% of unconstrained rewrites contain semantic drift that corrupts supervision and weakens generalization. We formalize this problem as instruction supervision instability and propose a data-centric stabilization recipe that jointly improves coverage and fidelity through three mechanisms: controllable instruction diversification for systematic expansion, LLM-based drift filtering for quality control, and attribute-aligned supervision that grounds prosody control in acoustic perturbations. On the Chinese split of InstructTTSEval, our recipe raises instruction-following from 34.5% without fine-tuning and 51.0% with naive fine-tuning to 56.4%, while constrained rewriting reduces drift from 40.4% to 15.4%. Ablations confirm the three mechanisms are complementary, and the drift taxonomy may generalize to instruction-driven generation beyond TTS. 1
column7: Yizhong Geng(Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Kecan Mao(Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Qifei Li(Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Cong Wang(Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Yingming Gao(Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications); Ruimin Wang(Li Auto); Chunfeng Wang(Li Auto); Hao Li(Li Auto); Ya Li(Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications)

column4: Improving Stable Speech Synthesis Post-Training with ChatScorer and Margin-Based Preference Construction
column6: Existing post-training methods for codec-based text-to-speech (TTS) often rely on multiple automatic metrics, such as character or word error rate (CER/WER) for content consistency, speaker similarity (SIM) for speaker preservation, and their weighted combinations as reward signals. However, directly fusing heterogeneous metrics into a single scalar reward can yield weakly separated candidate scores, leading to ambiguous supervision. In this paper, we propose a new post-training framework for stable speech synthesis, which introduces ChatScorer as an auxiliary reward model and combines it with margin-based preference construction. We instantiate the proposed framework using different post-training methods, and experiments on codec-based TTS show that it reduces undesirable outputs and improves generation stability, while maintaining competitive intelligibility and speaker similarity.
column7: Shihao Niu(Tianjin University); Jianguo Wei(Tianjin University); Wenhuan Lu(Tianjin University); Xianghu Yue(Tianjin University); Wei Li(Banma Network Technology Co., Ltd.); Ming Zhou(Banma Network Technology Co., Ltd.); Ming Cai(Banma Network Technology Co., Ltd.); Luo Si(Banma Network Technology Co., Ltd.)

column4: Accent-Emotion Entanglement in LM-Based Text-to-Speech Systems
column6: Speaker similarity metrics (SSM) are widely used for quick and easy evaluation of zero-shot text-to-speech (ZS-TTS) systems. However, using a case study of two ZS-TTS systems that have comparable SSM, we show such metrics may fail to capture important speech characteristics such as accent, and that relying on them can hide errors. We identify a phenomenon termed accent-emotion entanglement, whereby emotion conditioning can unintentionally alter accent, which is not reflected in previously reported high speaker similarity scores. We evaluate the systems with accent SMOS listening tests, and visualisation and cosine-distance analysis of embeddings. One has substantial accent variability, with SMOS ranging from 1.17–4.13 and centroid cosine distances up to 0.06, while the other is stable. The results of our proposed approach highlight the limitations of standard speaker similarity metrics, and that targeted subjective and objective measures are needed to reveal hidden synthesis errors.
column7: Matthew Hayden(University of Edinburgh); Jinzuomu Zhong(University of Edinburgh); Korin Richmond(University of Edinburgh)

column4: How Do Instructions Shape Speech? Cross-Attention Attribution for Style-Captioned Text-to-Speech
column6: Style-captioned text-to-speech systems use natural language to control voice characteristics, but how individual words influence acoustic output remains unclear. Understanding this is critical for diagnosing failure modes and improving controllability in expressive TTS. We propose cross-attention attribution for speech diffusion models, adapting the DAAM framework to the speech domain for the first time, and apply it to CapSpeechTTS. Our method extracts per-token heatmaps across 25 layers and 24 ODE steps. We analyze 3,600 (style caption, text transcript) combinations comprising 120 style captions conditioning the generation of 30 text transcripts each, revealing how caption tokens shape waveforms. Results show: (1) style tokens have lower temporal variance than content/function tokens, confirming global conditioning; (2) style attention correlates with F0 and energy; (3) style conditioning peaks in early steps and deep layers; (4) attention entropy reaches its minimum at layer 17, co-occurring with the style importance peak, indicating maximal network selectivity at the most style-critical stage. This is the first study of how natural language influences cross-attention in speech diffusion models.
column7: Nityanand Mathur(Smallest.ai); Hamees Sayed(Smallest.ai); Wasim Madha(Smallest.ai); Apoorv Singh(Smallest.ai); Sameer Khurana(Smallest.ai); Akshat Mandloi(Smallest.ai); Sudarshan Kamath(Smallest.ai)

column4: Beyond Two-stage Diffusion TTS: Joint Structure and Content Refinement via Jump Diffusion
column6: Diffusion and flow matching TTS faces a tension between discrete temporal structure and continuous spectral modeling. Two-stage models diffuse on fixed alignments, often collapsing to mean prosody; single-stage models avoid explicit durations but suffer alignment instability. We propose a jump-diffusion framework where discrete jumps model temporal structure and continuous diffusion refines spectral content within one process. Even in its one-shot degenerate form, our framework achieves 3.37% WER vs. 4.38% for Grad-TTS with improved UTMOSv2 on LJSpeech. The full iterative UDD variant further enables adaptive prosody, autonomously inserting natural pauses in out-of-distribution slow speech rather than stretching uniformly. Audio samples are available at https://anonymousinterpseech.github.io/TTS_Demo/.
column7: Jiabao Ai(The University of Sheffield); Minghui Zhao(The University of Sheffield); Anton Ragni(The University of Sheffield)

column4: PhonemeCVAE: Contrastive Latent Clustering with Class-Conditioned Priors for Controllable Phoneme Interpolation
column6: In order to achieve precise pronunciation control, high-quality TTS systems rely on structured and disentangled speech representations. We propose PhonemeCVAE, a phoneme-conditioned variational autoencoder that learns a structured continuous latent space for phoneme-level representations. The model introduces class-conditioned Gaussian priors for each phoneme and employs a contrastive objective to promote compact intra-class clustering and clear phoneme class disentanglement. The resulting latent space enables controllable phoneme modifications via interpolation at inference time, allowing smooth transitions between phonological classes and semantically meaningful modifications of synthesized speech. Furthermore, the combination of contrastive regularization and phoneme-conditioned priors forms a structured latent topology in the VAE that generalizes across English speech datasets, supporting consistent phoneme interpolation without compromising synthesis quality.
column7: Nina Goes(Department for Artificial Intelligence in Biomedical Engineering, Erlangen-Nürnberg); Lars Meyer(Max Planck Institute); Katrin Neumann(University Hospital Münster); Paula Andrea Pérez-Toro(Friedrich-Alexander Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg); Andreas M. Kist(Department for Artificial Intelligence in Biomedical Engineering, Erlangen-Nürnberg)

column4: TAP-ETS: Time Aligned Phoneme Guiding for EMG-to-Speech Synthesis
column6: Electromyography (EMG)-to-speech (ETS) synthesis generates speech from articulatory muscle activity without acoustic input. We propose TAP-ETS, a time-aligned phoneme guiding framework that conditions mel-spectrogram generation on frame-wise phoneme sequences through cross-attention. Unlike prior work that treats phonemes as auxiliary supervision, our model injects aligned phoneme embeddings directly into the decoder. We also introduce refinement strategies that redistribute merged semantic guidance over frame-wise EMG signals, enabling the seamless integration of arbitrary phoneme-or text-level correction methods without modifying the synthesis model. On the Gaddy silent EMG benchmark, TAP-ETS reduces WER from 25.12% to 19.77%, achieving state-of-the-art performance and demonstrating the importance of accurate frame-level alignment.
column7: Dongyub Han(Seoul National University); Injune Hwang(Seoul National University); Jaejun Lee(Seoul National University); Jiwon Lee(Seoul National University); Kyogu Lee(Seoul National University)

column4: Transitional Objective Learning with Connectionist Temporal Classification in Phoneme Recognition
column6: Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) is widely used for phoneme recognition due to its alignment-free training objective, but it often produces highly peaky posterior distributions dominated by the blank token. This is particularly challengingduring early training, when phonemes compete against strong blank token dominance and unstable alignment dynamics. We propose Transitional Objective Learning (TOL), a curriculum-learning framework that mitigates this issue by dynamically transitioning between training objectives of increasing granularity. Instead of optimizing a fine-grained phoneme objective throughout training, TOL begins with coarse-grained phonetic objectives that provide stable learning signals and gradually shifts toward full phoneme-level supervision. Experiments on English, French, and Polish show that TOL consistently reduces Phoneme Error Rate (PER), accelerates convergence, and improves training stability compared to conventional CTC fine-tuning.
column7: Izabela Krysińska(Poznan University of Technology; Pearson Central Europe); Mikołaj Morzy(Poznan University of Technology); Agnieszka Pludra(Pearson Central Europe)

column4: Align-Consistency: Improving Non-autoregressive and Semi-supervised ASR with Consistency Regularization
column6: Consistency regularization (CR) improves the robustness and accuracy of Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC) by ensuring predictions remain stable across input perturbations. In this work, we propose Align-Consistency, an extension of CR designed for Align-Refine--a non-autoregressive (non-AR) model that performs iterative refinement of frame-level hypotheses. This method leverages the speed of parallel inference while significantly boosting recognition performance. The effectiveness of Align-Consistency is demonstrated in two settings. First, in the fully supervised setting, our results indicate that applying CR to both the base CTC model and the subsequent refinement steps is critical, and the accuracy improvements from non-AR decoding and CR are mutually additive. Second, for semi-supervised ASR, we employ fast non-AR decoding to generate online pseudo-labels on unlabeled data, which are used to further refine the supervised model and lead to substantial gains.
column7: Wanting Huang(University of Iowa); Weiran Wang(University of Iowa)

column4: COALA: Robust Contextualized Speech-augmented Language Modeling for ASR via Contrastive Regularizer and Biasing Score Estimation
column6: Contextual biasing seeks to integrate external knowledge into automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems to accurately recognize domain-specific entities. In this paper, we propose COALA1 (COntextualized ASR Leveraging biAsing scoring), a robust framework designed to enhance speech-augmented language models (SLMs) in complex multi-entity scenarios. Considering the inherent context-window limitations of SLMs, identifying relevant target entities from a large-scale biasing list is crucial for effective recognition. To this end, COALA maps SLM latent representations into a specialized discriminative space to quantify the matching intensity between audio segments and candidate entities. Furthermore, we address the training collapse in prior study when handling multi-target utterances—where multiple rare words co-occur. Experimental results on the LibriSpeech benchmark demonstrate that COALA consistently achieves superior contextual biasing performance across various biasing list scales.
column7: Jhih-Rong Guo(National Taiwan Normal University); Bi-Cheng Yan(National Taiwan Normal University); Tien-Hong Lo(National Taiwan Normal University); Berlin Chen(National Taiwan Normal University)

column4: UGPCB: Uncertainty-Gated Phonetic Contextual Biasing for Improving Hotword Recognition in Large Speech Models
column6: Automatic speech recognition systems exhibit recognition bias when processing hot words. Context bias techniques effectively tackle this issue by integrating user-defined vocabularies, thus enhancing keyword transcription accuracy. Although speech matching technology has advanced context bias techniques by resolving subword fragmentation, existing methods still face challenges with over-bias and homophone misclassification. To address this, this study proposes a training-free decode-time framework named Uncertainty-Gated Phonetic Contextual Bias (UGPCB). This framework employs an entropy-driven gating mechanism and bimodal contrastive penalties, and it is evaluated on the Dolphin base model. The experimental results demonstrate a 16.04% recall improvement (achieving an F1 score of 90.81%) while restricting precision reduction to 0.78%. Even when 1,000 distractors are introduced, the recall still increases by 14.26%, fully demonstrating the method's potential for ASR applications.
column7: Yong-Jie Hou(Tsinghua University; Tiangong University); Yun-Fei Shao(Tsinghua University); Wei-Qiang Zhang(Tsinghua University)

column4: Refining the Latent Bridge: Superior ASR Performance via Adapter-Only Alignment with Diffusion LLMs
column6: In this work, we validate a parameter-efficient approach to Speech-LLM based ASR that enforces a strict adapter-only alignment protocol. Unlike existing methods that rely on full-parameter or partial backbone updates, we keep both the speech encoder and the LLM frozen, focusing exclusively on the adapter as the sole learnable interface. We demonstrate that this restricted alignment strategy, though often underexplored, is particularly effective for Diffusion-based LLMs. Our results show that Diffusion models are significantly more resilient to the adapter-only bottleneck than Autoregressive (AR) models, yielding higher Real-Time Factors (RTF) and superior ASR performance across various data size splits. While AR models suffer from error propagation and drift when denied full-parameter tuning, the global refinement mechanism of Diffusion proves more scalable and efficient for multimodal LLM integration.
column7: Puneet Singh Bhooi(IIIT-Delhi); Vinayak Abrol(IIIT-Delhi)

column4: DASH: Dual-View Self-Distillation with Multi-Layer Hidden Representations for Robust Speech Recognition
column6: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) often degrades in real-world noisy environments, making noise robustness essential for deployment. Supervised noise-augmented fine-tuning is a common remedy, but it can introduce a robustness-clean trade-off and overfit to specific corruptions, degrading recognition in clean conditions. We propose DASH, a self-distillation framework that improves robustness by learning clean-noisy consistency from paired views. DASH distills hidden representations from multiple encoder layers to capture features from low-level acoustics to high-level semantics, and stabilizes training by minimizing KL divergence between prototype assignment distributions of clean and noisy views. Experiments on LibriSpeech show that DASH consistently improves recognition under diverse noisy conditions while preserving clean accuracy, achieved by a label-free pre-training stage with minimal additional overhead (about 4% of fine-tuning time) beyond standard fine-tuning.
column7: Jaeeun Baik(Sogang University); Ui-Hyeop Shin(Sogang University); Jiwon Lee(Sogang University); Woocheol Jeong(Sogang University); Hyung-Min Park(Sogang University)

column4: Whisper-Aware LLM: Self-Supervised Uncertainty Learning for Robust Whispered Speech Recognition
column6: The signal ambiguity of whispered speech drives ASR systems toward two opposing failure modes: failing to capture whispered speech or hallucinatory transcription of noise. This paper introduces the Whisper-Aware LLM, a framework that teaches an Audio-LLM to perceive and react to this uncertainty. Our model develops an intrinsic self-awareness by learning to quantify the physical deficiencies of acoustic signals through targeted self-supervised tasks. This learned uncertainty is then operationalized via a novel Confidence-Fused Decoding mechanism, which provides both high-level instructions and frame-level attention modulation to the LLM decoder. Our experiments confirm the effectiveness of this approach. The model sets a new state-of-the-art on whispered speech with a 17% relative CER reduction on AISHELL6-Whisper. At the same time, it directly addresses the reliability trade-off, with hallucination rates dropping from over 25% to 4.5%.
column7: Gaopeng Xu(Alibaba); Zhenyu Wang(Alibaba); Zheng Xue(Alibaba); Yinfeng Xia(Alibaba); Haitao Yao(Alibaba)

column4: Probing and Mitigating Hallucinations in Speech-augmented Language Models for Automatic Speech Recognition via Small Language Models
column6: The widespread success of large language models in natural language processing has spurred the development of speech-augmented language models (SLMs) to extend their reasoning capabilities from textual inputs to spoken ones. Despite impressive performance, SLMs remain susceptible to hallucinations, posing challenges in practical utility. To this end, we first probe hallucinations in SLMs for automatic speech recognition (ASR) via the lens of causal mediation and behavioral analysis. To mitigate fabricated ASR hypotheses, we propose AudioSLM, a compact yet effective ASR framework built upon a small language model, which leverages alignment cues and cross-attention layers to synergistically bolster acoustic modeling and cross-modal interactions. Experiments on LibriSpeech reveal that hallucinations arise from multi-head self-attention modules with an excessive attention bias towards textual tokens. AudioSLM considerably eases ASR hallucinations and outperforms some LLM-based ASR models.
column7: Bi-Cheng Yan(National Taiwan Normal University); Jhih-Rong Guo(National Taiwan Normal University); Fu-An Chao(National Taiwan Normal University); Berlin Chen(National Taiwan Normal University)

column4: Rank-Distance Based Confidence Estimation for ASR
column6: Confidence scores in Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) are required to assess the correctness of the predicted text. Class probabilities from overconfident ASR decoders do not reflect prediction accuracy. Auxiliary Confidence Estimation Model (CEM) based on binary target scores does not reflect the correctness of partially correct transcripts. CEM based on temporal continuous target scores suffers from inaccurate alignment. We observe the diminishing class probabilities in true-class probability-based CEM. To address the limitations of the State-of-the-Art (SOTA) CEM, we propose a novel continuous target score, named RanD. Then, we present RanD-based CEM for four ASR architectures: Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC), Recurrent Neural Network-Transducer (RNN-T), Token Duration Transducer (TDT), and Attention-based Encoder Decoder (AED). Experiments with Hindi and English ASR show that our approach outperforms SOTA CEM and also generalises to mismatched domains.
column7: Nagarathna Ravi(CSIR Fourth Paradigm Institute); Madduri Aiswarya Lakshmi(CSIR Fourth Paradigm Institute); Ragesh M(CSIR Fourth Paradigm Institute); Rajalakshmi Elangovan(CSIR Fourth Paradigm Institute)

column4: Training-Free Intelligibility-Guided Observation Addition for Noisy ASR
column6: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) degrades severely in noisy environments. Although speech enhancement (SE) front-ends effectively suppress background noise, they often introduce artifacts that harm recognition. Observation addition (OA) addressed this issue by fusing noisy and SE enhanced speech, improving recognition without modifying the parameters of the SE or ASR models. This paper proposes an intelligibility-guided OA method, where fusion weights are derived from intelligibility estimates obtained directly from the backend ASR. Unlike prior OA methods based on trained neural predictors, the proposed method is training-free, reducing complexity and enhances generalization. Extensive experiments across diverse SE-ASR combinations and datasets demonstrate strong robustness and improvements over existing OA baselines. Additional analyses of intelligibility-guided switching-based alternatives and frame versus utterance-level OA further validate the proposed design.
column7: Haoyang Li(Nanyang Technological University); Changsong Liu(Nanyang Technological University); Wei Rao(Nanyang Technological University); Hao Shi(Independent Researcher); Sakriani Sakti(Nara Institute of Science and Technology); Eng Siong Chng(Nanyang Technological University)

column4: Beyond WER: Entity and Disfluency Recall in Accented Conversational ASR
column6: ASR systems optimised for Word Error Rate (WER) often miss named entities and filled pauses in accented conversational English, both critical for language-learning feedback. We present a three-stage pipeline for speakers from India, Indonesia, and Latin America: (1) heuristic SQL filters curating entity-rich training data at ~2.8× the entity density of random sampling, (2) regional LoRA adapters fine-tuned on Qwen2.5-Omni-3B producing both verbatim and corrected transcripts in a single forward pass, and (3) a six-category error taxonomy validated by an LLM-based judge (83.8% agreement, 210 human-labelled samples). The pipeline achieves 80-85% entity recall (up from 53-55%), 76-86% filler recall (up from <5%), and 6-10% WER across 6 k test utterances, outperforming Whisper and a commercial ASR on entity recall while matching a zero-shot 30B model with 10 x fewer parameters. Paired bootstrap tests confirm that curation alone accounts for 2.8-4.2 pp of entity recall gain (p < 0.0001).
column7: Fiza Husain(Stimuler); Ankit Pandey(Stimuler); Yash Singh(Stimuler)

column4: Exploring Hesitation as a Signal for Spoken Grammatical Error Correction
column6: Traditional spoken GEC pipelines treat disfluencies as noise to be removed before correction. We challenge this assumption for L2 learner speech, hypothesizing that disfluencies signal grammatical uncertainty and provide valuable cues for error correction. We propose a novel hesitation-aware approach that preserves disfluency information via: (1) special marker tokens indicating hesitation positions and types, and (2) hesitation type embeddings that encode disfluency context. Experiments on the Speak & Improve Corpus 2025 show that our method outperforms both rule-based disfluency removal (+2.05%p) and human-annotated fluent transcription (+1.84%p) in F0.5, with gains particularly pronounced near hesitation positions (+2.78%p), demonstrating that disfluencies carry informative signals for spoken GEC and should be leveraged rather than discarded.
column7: Seunghoon Han(Tutorus Labs Inc.); Minyoung Kyoung(Tutorus Labs Inc.); Hyungbae Jeon(Tutorus Labs Inc.)

column4: Discriminating Proficiency Levels in L2 Speech: A Comparative Study of Self-Supervised Models in Basque
column6: Automated speaking assessment is crucial for computer-assisted language learning applications. Research has mainly focused on intermediate proficiency levels in languages with many L2 learners, predominantly English, where learner corpora are available. For low-resource languages lacking large annotated corpora, models based on self-supervised learning can help overcome this problem. In this work, we investigate whether multilingual self-supervised speech models can effectively discriminate C1-level proficiency in Basque, a low-resource language, and show that mHuBERT-147 achieves a statistically significant improvement over wav2vec 2.0 xlsr. To illustrate reproducibility, we replicate our experiments in the ICNALE corpus of L2 English, providing a complementary perspective in different linguistic and proficiency contexts.
column7: Christoforos Souganidis(University of the Basque Country); Aitor Bellanco(HiTZ Basque Center for Language TeUniversity of the Basque Country); Andoni Sudupe(University of the Basque Country); Inma Hernáez(University of the Basque Country); Ibon Saratxaga(University of the Basque Country); Eva Navas(University of the Basque Country)

column4: A Multi-Agent Framework to Automate Feedback Generation for IELTS Speaking Test using Multimodal SpeechLMs
column6: Automated speaking assessment aims to align evaluations with human judgments. Current regression-based scoring models that rely on handcrafted linguistic features suffer from poor construct coverage and centralised scores, while automatic speech recognition (ASR) methods impose an informational bottleneck by overlooking acoustic and prosodic nuances that are indispensable for analysing fluency and pronunciation. This paper proposes a multi-agent framework using multimodal SpeechLMs for the IELTS Speaking test. By performing direct analysis of the audio without intermediate transcription, it jointly models acoustic-prosodic and linguistic information via four role-based agents that mirror each scoring criterion. Results on a newly built benchmark dataset of IELTS speaking mock tests show that the system achieves higher scoring correlation with human examiners compared to a regression model baseline, while generating reports that exhibit greater semantic similarity to expert feedback.
column7: Hui Xin Koh(The University of Manchester); Yang Wang(The University of Manchester); Chenghua Lin(The University of Manchester)

column4: A Finetuned SpeechLLM for Joint Multi-Granular L2 Assessment and Natural-Language Rationales
column6: Automated L2 speech assessment can assign proficiency labels, but often lacks interpretability. We propose a rubric-guided SpeechLLM for multi-aspect, multi-granular assessment, trained with a hybrid objective combining supervised fine-tuning and Bounded Direct Preference Optimization. The model jointly predicts ordinal labels at the sentence-level (accuracy, fluency, prosody), word/phoneme-level accuracy, and generates a natural-language rationale in the same response. On SpeechOcean762, our approach matches or outperforms single-granularity models while remaining competitive with prior approaches. We analyze rationale reliability along two axes: self-consistency with model predictions and alignment with ground-truth labels, using sentiment consistency (plausibility) and mention-based agreement (faithfulness). Rationales are plausible at the sentence level, but faithfulness degrades at the word/phoneme level: references are sparse and weakly aligned with token-level labels.
column7: Aditya Kamlesh Parikh(Radboud University); Cristian Tejedor Garcia(Radboud University); Catia Cucchiarini(Radboud University); Helmer Strik(Radboud University)

column4: LOPA: Enhancing Spoken Language Assessment via Latent Ordinal Prototype Alignment
column6: Fueled by increasing model scale and multimodal inputs, Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for Spoken Language Assessment (SLA). While effective, this paradigm often overlooks the intrinsic ordinal structure of language acquisition. This paper works around the necessity of large-scale MLLMs by introducing Latent Ordinal Prototype Alignment (LOPA) for SLA, a prototype-based regularizer that enforces an ordinal geometric prior directly on the latent space. Coupled with Semantic-Anchored Layer Routing (SALR), which adaptively harvests multi-depth representations from a frozen Whisper encoder, our framework achieves an RMSE of 0.361. This performance rivals billion-parameter systems without the need for LLM-based fine-tuning. Further analysis reveals that SALR's synergy with LOPA offers interpretable, criterion-aligned preferences, thereby supporting an efficient and ordinal-aware modeling alternative to current scaling-centric models for SLA.
column7: Hong-Yun Lin(National Taiwan Normal University); Fu-An Chao(National Taiwan Normal University); Bi-Cheng Yan(National Taiwan Normal University); Berlin Chen(National Taiwan Normal University)

column4: Adaptive Multimodal Expert Specialization by Meta-Learning for Spoken English Assessment
column6: In the conversational artificial intelligence era, a learner's voice is vital, yet automated scoring often fails to capture them due to data scarcity and privacy constraints. We propose a meta-learning-based framework for adaptive multimodal expert specialization, transforming the system into an adaptive listener. Instead of a one-size-fits-all model, our approach uses a mixture of experts architecture in which subnetworks learn to specialize in diverse vocal profiles. This synergy enables the model to rapidly "learn to learn" from limited samples, thus providing a personalized and accurate reflection of a speaker's true capabilities. Our framework achieves an F1-score greater than 84% in classification and a mean squared error of 0.225 in regression. By optimizing deep model performance under extreme data constraints, this framework offers a robust, scalable solution for automated English coaching that balances adaptation with predictive accuracy. Our code is publicly available.
column7: Cong-Thanh Vu(JAIST); Candy Olivia Mawalim(JAIST); Hung Le(JAIST); Chee Wee Leong(ETS); Guy Sivan(Vericant.com); Shogo Okada(JAIST)

column4: Using Phonological-Level Wav2Vec2 for Mandarin Automatic Mispronunciation Detection and Diagnosis
column6: Automatic mispronunciation detection and diagnosis (MDD) plays a crucial role in L2 Mandarin pronunciation learning. While end-to-end (E2E) based MDD methods have substantially improved phoneme-level detection accuracy, diagnostic feedback remains limited, as segmental and tonal errors are not explicitly separated. In this paper, we propose a phonological feature-based MDD framework that models both segmental and tonal attributes within a unified Wav2Vec2-CTC architecture. Experimental results show that the proposed method reduces False Acceptance Rate (FAR) by 10.1% and Diagnostic Error Rate (DER) by 23.6% compared with the phoneme-only baseline system. By decomposing phonemes into low-level phonological components, the proposed approach enables more detailed and interpretable diagnostic feedback for L2 learners.
column7: Jinghao Chen(UNSW Sydney); Mostafa Shahin(UNSW Sydney); Beena Ahmed(UNSW Sydney)

column4: Domain-Aware Mispronunciation Detection and Diagnosis Using Language-Specific Statistical Graphs
column6: Mispronunciation Detection and Diagnosis (MDD) has gained increasing importance in computer-assisted language learning and speech technology in recent years. In this paper, we propose a method for constructing statistical graphs that enable models to learn phoneme confusion patterns represented as directed graphs. Furthermore, we introduce a language-specific strategy to capture systematic pronunciation differences across various native language (L1) backgrounds. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through extensive experiments on the L2-ARCTIC benchmark, where it achieves an F1-score of 59.52%, outperforming several competitive baselines.
column7: Hanh Nguyen(NEU); Tuong Tu Huu(VNPT AI; HUST); Huan Vu(NEU, VNPT AI); Thien Van Luong(NEU, VNPT AI); Tien Cuong Nguyen(VNPT AI); Thi Thu Trang Nguyen(HUST)

column4: Light-weight Pronunciation Assessment via Discrete Speech Token Surprisal
column6: Training automated pronunciation assessment often relies on labeled learner errors or non-native corpora that are costly to collect. We propose a lightweight framework trained only on native speech resources, operating unsupervised or lightly calibrated with a small set of scored utterances. At inference, learner speech is discretized with an SSL encoder and a K-means codebook. A token language model trained on native sequences computes surprisal where higher surprisal indicates phonotactic deviation. We add a transcript-guided Text2DUnit–DTW module that predicts native token sequences from reference text and aligns them to acoustic tokens to derive error-sensitive features. Surprisal and alignment features are fused via simple regression. On SpeechOcean762, PCC improves from 0.60 to 0.66 with transcript guidance, near supervised baselines. Cross-dataset evaluation on L2-ARCTIC shows consistent gains.
column7: Syeda Faiza Ahmed Sara(Qatar Computing Research Institute); Shammur Absar Chowdhury(Qatar Computing Research Institute)

column4: ALFreeD: Teacher-Guided Few-Shot Pronunciation Assessment via Segmentation-Free Deviation Modeling
column6: Automatic pronunciation assessment (APA) of L2 learners is critical in computer-assisted language learning. Existing approaches typically rely on canonical phonemes, its aligned boundaries and large labeled data, which is costly and cumbersome. To address these, we propose ALFreeD, a segmentation-free APA framework guided by teacher's speech without the need of canonical phonemes using minimal labeled data. In this, pronunciation quality is assessed by quantifying deviation between learners' and teacher's utterances. First, frame-level embeddings are extracted using HuBERT, and deviation scores are computed between them after obtaining their temporal correspondence with DTW. Next, utterance level pronunciation deviation vector is obtained by suppressing variabilities other than pronunciation quality with i-vector framework and is passed to a MLP for predicting quality. Experiments on SpeechOcean762 demonstrate competitive performance with recent E2E methods using minimal labeled data.
column7: Meenakshi Sirigiraju(IIITH); Nevin K Mathew(Saintgits College of Engineering); Reni K Cherian(Saintgits College of Engineering); Chiranjeevi Yarra(IIITH)

column4: Automatic Assessment of L2 Speech Intelligibility: Segmental Error Ranking
column6: Current CAPT systems prioritize identification and correction of all learner deviations from native speech, thereby overlooking the main goal of language acquisition: effective communication. In response, we propose an intelligibility-centered approach, which targets only selected segmental aspects of speech influencing communicative effectiveness. We employ a regression model based on phoneme substitution errors. Using AdaBoost feature importance, we propose an intelligibility-based ranking of segmental errors, shedding light on the relationship between the mispronunciation of individual phonemes and overall speech intelligibility. This approach, validated on human ratings of speech samples from VoxPopuli, speechocean762, and an internal dataset, not only predicts intelligibility levels but also directs ESL learners toward the acquisition of the most critical phonemes. By foregrounding intelligibility over nativeness, it supports more learner-centered and inclusive CAPT solutions.
column7: Agnieszka Pludra(Pearson Central Europe); Izabela Krysińska(Pearson Central Europe); Matuesz Jekiel(Adam Mickiewicz University)

column4: A System-Agnostic Approach to Modelling Interaction Quality in Spoken Dialogue Systems
column6: Previous studies have used system-dependent (SD) input features, such as system log data, and machine learning to automatically evaluate user interactions with spoken dialogue systems. However, this approach lacks generalisability across different systems. This study implements a system-agnostic (SA) approach, using acoustic, textual and temporal features to model interaction quality (IQ). Across two experimental phases, we compare the performance of IQ classifiers trained on static and fine-tuned SD and SA features. We found that while the SD features were superior in a static pipeline, the SA features achieved comparable performance when end-to-end fine-tuning was employed. Therefore, our results demonstrate that SA features, when fine-tuned, offer a viable, system-independent alternative for IQ modelling, enabling more scalable evaluations across different dialogue systems.
column7: Paul Gering(University of Sheffield); Roger K. Moore(University of Sheffield)

column4: Considerate Listener Modeling for Korean Streaming Backchannel Prediction
column6: Mistimed backchannels can interrupt ongoing speech and degrade user experience. A Considerate Listener concentrates backchannel interventions near pause-proximate regions in real time, since backchannels cluster around speaker pauses. However, not all pauses invite a backchannel. Pauses that follow utterances calling for a reply may be pragmatically inappropriate for backchannel intervention. Acoustic cues alone may not capture the linguistic context needed to distinguish these cases, so acoustic-only predictors tend to over-predict. We therefore propose a zero look-ahead streaming backchannel predictor combining pause-aware soft scaling with Q-Former fusion of partial ASR hypotheses. We introduce Semantic False Discovery Rate (Semantic FDR) to quantify backchannel predictions in pragmatically inappropriate pause regions. On a Korean counseling corpus, our approach reduces Semantic FDR by 53.8% and improves Macro-F1 by 2.16 pp compared to an acoustic-only baseline.
column7: Yong-Seok Choi(Electronics and Telecommunications Research Institute); Seung Hi Kim(Electronics and Telecommunications Research Institute); Sung Yup Lee(Electronics and Telecommunications Research Institute)

column4: Context Projector: Complementary Keyword and Dialogue Context Embeddings for LLM-based ASR
column6: Contact-center dialogue systems require both accurate transcripts and reliable recognition of business-critical entities. We introduce a hybrid keyword and context projector (CP) approach for LLM-based ASR. Rather than appending raw dialogue history, CP encodes previous turns into compact contextual tokens, complemented by automatically extracted keywords. The module is trained while keeping the backbone frozen, enabling parameter-efficient adaptation. Experiments on realistic, multi-domain contact-center data show that naive raw-context prompting can degrade performance, whereas the proposed approach improves the tradeoff between overall and bias-word error, achieving average relative reductions of up to 2.5% overall and 7.2% on bias words. These results show our approach to be an effective and practical enhancement of context-aware LLM-based ASR.
column7: Esaú Villatoro-Tello(Idiap Research Institute); Sergio Burdisso(Idiap Research Institute); Shashi Kumar(Idiap Research Institute; EPFL); Hasindri Watawana(Idiap Research Institute; EPFL); Srikanth Madikeri(University of Zurich); Manjunath K E(Uniphore); Jeena Prakash(Uniphore); Thibault Bañeras-Roux(Idiap Research Institute); Kadri Hacioglu(Uniphore); Petr Motlicek(Idiap Research Institute; Brno University of Technology); Andreas Stolcke(Uniphore)

column4: DP-BCT: A Dual-Path model for predicting BackChannel Timing
column6: Backchannel timing prediction is challenging because responses occur at varying latencies relative to Backchannel Opportunity Points (BOPs). Dual-Process Theory motivates testing whether backchannel fast/slow functional categories exhibit distinct BOP-relative latency distributions; where BOP-relative latency is the signed interval between a BOP and an annotated backchannel onset. Using K-MIND, a 115-hour Korean dyadic corpus, Cox Proportional Hazards analysis confirms significant differences in BOP-relative latency distributions across four functional categories (all p < .001), supporting a DPT-based fast group/slow group distinction. Based on this result, the Dual-Path Backchannel Timing Prediction Model (DP-BCT) decouples the fast/slow groups into the Fast Path and Slow Path for frame-level onset and functional category prediction. DP-BCT improves backchannel timing prediction accuracy over SP-BCT, a single-path baseline, raising Macro-F1 from 0.4862 to 0.6254.
column7: Jin Yea Jang(Seoul National University; Korea Electronics Technology Institute); Saim Shin(Korea Electronics Technology Institute); Gahgene Gweon(Seoul National University)

column4: From Awareness to Adherence: Bridging the Context Gap in Spoken Dialogue Systems via Context-Aware Decoding
column6: Despite the success of end-to-end (E2E) spoken dialogue systems, maintaining strict context adherence in multi-round conversations remains a challenge. While prior works attribute these failures to models forgetting dialogue history, we highlight an equally critical but overlooked bottleneck: a gap between latent context awareness and active adherence. Although models internally recognize relevant past utterances, strong parametric priors often overshadow these signals during decoding. To bridge this gap, we propose an audio-adapted Context-Aware Decoding (CAD) approach. By leveraging internal attention mechanisms to isolate key historical rounds, our approach contrasts output distributions with and without this key context during inference, directly amplifying multimodal contextual signals. Evaluations on the Audio MultiChallenge benchmark demonstrate significant improvements in Semantic Memory and Self Coherence subtasks, successfully enforcing strict, context-faithful adherence.
column7: Che Hyun Lee(Seoul National University); Heeseung Kim(University of Seoul); Sungroh Yoon(Seoul National University)

column4: From Reactive to Proactive: Assessing the Proactivity of Voice Agents via ProVoice-Bench
column6: Recent advancements in LLM agents are gradually shifting from reactive, text-based paradigms toward proactive, multimodal interaction. However, existing benchmarks primarily focus on reactive responses, overlooking the complexities of proactive intervention and monitoring. To bridge this gap, we introduce ProVoice-Bench, the first evaluation framework specifically designed for proactive voice agents, featuring four novel tasks. By leveraging a multi-stage data synthesis pipeline, we curate 1,182 high-quality samples for rigorous testing. Our evaluation of state-of-the-art Multimodal LLMs reveals a significant performance gap, particularly regarding over-triggering and reasoning capabilities. These findings highlight the limitations of current models and offer a roadmap for developing more natural, context-aware proactive agents.
column7: Ke Xu(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Yuhao Wang(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Yu Wang(Shanghai Jiao Tong University)

column4: Integrating Facial Generation into Full-Duplex Spoken Dialogue Systems
column6: Full-duplex spoken dialogue models, such as Moshi, enable natural, low-latency voice conversations. However, they remain limited to the audio modality, lacking the facial expressions that are integral to human communication. We present Moshi-Face, the first full-duplex dialogue model that jointly processes the user's audio and facial input while simultaneously generating speech and facial motion. We first construct a vector-quantized variational autoencoder (VQ-VAE) as a face codec that encodes 3D head meshes extracted from facial videos into compact discrete tokens, referred to as face tokens, and conversely reconstructs 3D meshes from these tokens. We then extend Moshi with a Face Transformer module that generates face tokens non-autoregressively, enabling Moshi-Face to produce synchronized audio and face tokens in real time. Experiments show that Moshi-Face achieves audiovisual alignment at low latency while preserving the dialogue quality of the original audio-only model.
column7: Jingjing Jiang(Nagoya University); Atsumoto Ohashi(Nagoya University); Ryuichiro Higashinaka(Nagoya University)

column4: Optimal Linguistic Complexity for Dialogue System Speech in Noise: Convergent Evidence from Automatic and Human Transcription
column6: Spoken dialogue systems must synthesise responses that are reliably understood in noisy conditions, yet the optimal linguistic complexity for both ASR and human listeners remains empirically underexplored. We address this gap with two studies. Study 1 measured ASR accuracy for 168,000 synthesised utterances spanning five complexity levels, two TTS systems, twelve noise types, and seven SNRs. Study 2 (pilot, N = 15) had human listeners transcribe synthesised utterances at three complexity levels across four noise environments and three SNRs. Both studies show a U-shaped pattern: natural grammatical sentences (Level 3, 9–16 words) outperform telegraphic forms (Level 1) by 43% in ASR WER and by 45% in human transcription error. The grammar advantage paradoxically grows as conditions improve. These findings reject adaptive simplification and establish a 9–19 words as optimal for system output.
column7: Lubos Marcinek(KTH Royal Institute of Technology); Jonas Beskow(KTH Royal Institute of Technology); Joakim Gustafson(KTH Royal Institute of Technology)

column4: Mitigating Scoring Errors and Compensating for Nonverbal Subtests in Speech-Based Dementia Assessment
column6: Early detection of cognitive impairment relies on neuropsychological tests to minimize subjectivity by assessing multiple cognitive domains. Speech-based evaluation can support diagnostics and improve accessibility, but transcription errors and the omission of nonverbal subtests (e.g., motor skills) limit accuracy. Beyond conventional test scores, speech-derived features can provide additional insights into cognitive status. This study investigates the speech-based evaluation of the German "Syndrom-Kurz-Test," a standardized dementia screening test comprising verbal and motor subtests. We train models that integrate transcript-derived scores and Whisper embeddings per verbal subtest to reduce scoring errors. To compensate for missing motor subtests, we then leverage these fused representations to approximate expert overall ratings. Despite omitting subtests, our models strongly correlate with expert ratings and efficiently and accurately discriminate between cognitive status groups.
column7: Franziska Braun(Technische Hochschule Nürnberg); Christopher Witzl(Technische Hochschule Nürnberg); Andreas Erzigkeit(Geromed GmbH); Hartmut Lehfeld(PMU Klinikum Nürnberg); Thomas Hillemacher(PMU Klinikum Nürnberg); Tobias Bocklet(Technische Hochschule Nürnberg); Korbinian Riedhammer(Technische Hochschule Nürnberg)

column4: HASS: Hierarchical Simulation of Logopenic Aphasic Speech for Scalable PPA Detection
column6: Building a diagnosis model for primary progressive aphasia (PPA) has been challenging due to the data scarcity. Collecting clinical data at scale is limited by the high vulnerability of clinical population and the high cost of expert labeling. To circumvent this, previous studies simulate dysfluent speech to generate training data. However, those approaches are not comprehensive enough to simulate PPA as holistic, multi-level phenotypes, instead relying on isolated dysfluencies. To address this, we propose a novel, clinically grounded simulation framework, Hierarchical Aphasic Speech Simulation (HASS). HASS aims to simulate behaviors of logopenic variant of PPA (lvPPA) with varying degrees of severity. To this end, semantic, phonological, and temporal deficits of lvPPA are systematically identified by clinical experts, and simulated. We demonstrate that our framework enables more accurate and generalizable detection models. Code: anonymous.4open.science/r/HASS-890D
column7: Harrison Li(UC Berkeley); Kevin Wang(UC Berkeley); Cheol Jun Cho(UC Berkeley); Jiachen Lian(UC Berkeley); Rabab Rangwala(UCSF); Chenxu Guo(Zhejiang University); Emma Yang(Columbia University); Lynn Kurteff(UCSF); Zoe Ezzes(UCSF); Willa Keegan-Rodewald(UCSF); Jet Vonk(UCSF); Siddarth Ramkrishnan(UCSF); Giada Antonicelli(Basque Center on Cognition, Brain and Language); Zachary Miller(UCSF); Marilu Gorno Tempini(UCSF); Gopala Anumanchipalli(UC Berkeley)

column4: Listening Between the Lines: Joint Learning of ASR Embeddings and LLM-Augmented Linguistics for Dementia Detection
column6: Early detection of dementia through speech analysis offers a non-invasive screening alternative, but capturing both acoustic and linguistic biomarkers remains challenging. We propose a multimodal framework leveraging Whisper for dual-purpose extraction: acoustic representations from encoder outputs and transcripts via automatic speech recognition (ASR). For the acoustic pathway, temporal networks with attention pooling aggregate variable-length sequences into fixed-dimensional embeddings. For the linguistic pathway, we prompt a large language model (LLM) to extract interpretable features spanning lexical diversity, syntactic complexity, semantic coherence, and discourse patterns. A gated fusion network integrates both modalities. On ADReSS and ADReSSo, our method achieves F1-scores of 89.47% and 90.14%, demonstrating effective integration of acoustic and LLM-augmented linguistic features. Ablation shows that multimodal fusion consistently outperforms either modality alone.
column7: Olivier Jiyoun Jung(Ewha Womans University); Jonghyeon Park(NAVER Cloud); Myungwoo Oh(NAVER Cloud)

column4: LoRA-Tuned Large Language Models for Dementia Detection via Multi-View Speech-Derived Features
column6: Early detection of dementia enables timely intervention, and reflecting cognitive impairment, spontaneous speech offers a non-invasive screening modality. Conventional approaches often focus on a single representational dimension—such as acoustic descriptors, pause modeling, automatic speech recognition (ASR) transcripts, or multimodal fusion—limiting integrative reasoning across heterogeneous cognitive symptoms. We propose a low-rank adaptation (LoRA)-tuned large language model (LLM) that performs structured multi-view reasoning over four complementary speech-derived signals: ASR transcripts with pause markers, discourse-level topic cues, temporal fluency statistics, and phonological sequences. These cues are encoded within a unified prompt, enabling a single LLM to learn a coherent decision function without modality-specific encoders or late-stage fusion. On ADReSSo, our best model achieves an F1-score of 90.14%, and ablation confirms the complementary contribution of each view.
column7: Jonghyeon Park(NAVER Cloud); Olivier Jiyoun Jung(Ewha Womans University); Myungwoo Oh(NAVER Cloud)

column4: PAN-Mask: Pathology-Aware Neurological Masking with End-to-End Learnable Weights for Neurological Disorder Detection from Speech
column6: Self-supervised models like WavLM advance pathological speech classification but rely on content-agnostic random masking, which overlooks sparse, localized clinical biomarkers. We propose PAN-Mask (Pathology-Aware Neurological Masking), a task-aware regularization framework. A lightweight detector computes and aggregates six interpretable acoustic descriptors via learnable attention to estimate frame-level pathology salience. By selectively masking high-salience segments, PAN-Mask discourages shortcut learning and compels the encoder to capture robust, distributed representations. Joint optimization enables the model to learn task-discriminative patterns aligned with clinical biomarkers without manual design of feature importance. Evaluated on six datasets across three disorders and five languages using identical hyperparameters, PAN-Mask yields 8.31-22.72% accuracy gains (avg. 13.82%) over random masking and provides interpretable clinical insights.
column7: Qi Sun(Tsinghua University); Junhao Fan(Georgetown University); Boao Jing(Tsinghua University); Ziqi Chen(Tsinghua University); Guodong Lin(Tsinghua University); Wei-Qiang Zhang(Tsinghua University)

column4: Gated Multi-graph Fusion via Graph Attention Networks for Alzheimer’s Disease Detection
column6: Spontaneous speech is a vital non-invasive biomarker for Alzheimer’s Disease (AD), yet many systems overlook nonlinear structural disruptions and clinical heterogeneity in pathological language. We propose a Multi-View Gated Graph Attention Network that transcribes audio via Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) to construct semantic, dependency, and co-occurrence graphs, characterizing speech through a "content-structure-flow" framework. Notably, the co-occurrence graph leverages Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) from a normative corpus to quantify narrative logic and linguistic deviation. To address symptomatic diversity, an adaptive gated fusion mechanism dynamically integrates these views. Evaluated on the ADReSSo dataset, our model achieves 90.00% accuracy. Ablation results confirm that the PMI-based graph and heterogeneity-aware gating are essential for robust classification across diverse clinical populations. Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/opeacc/AD.
column7: Jinyu Li(Tianjin University); Xiao Wei(Tianjin University; Chinese Academy of Sciences); Bin Wen(Tianjin University, Chinese Academy of Sciences); Kai Li(Chinese Academy of Sciences); Yuqin Lin(Fuzhou University); Xiaobao Wang(Tianjin University); Longbiao Wang(Tianjin University, Huiyan Technology (Tianjin) Co., Ltd); Jianwu Dang(Chinese Academy of Sciences)

column4: From Echo to Accuracy: Robust Voice Quality Assessment Using Blind Unsupervised Diffusion-based Dereverberation
column6: Objective voice quality measures are sensitive to reverberation, which limits their robustness in clinical applications. This study investigates whether blind diffusion-based dereverberation enables room-independent assessment of voice quality using Smoothed Cepstral Peak Prominence (CPPS). Anechoic voice samples from two databases were convolved with impulse responses of real therapy rooms and subsequently dereverberated. Effects on CPPS level and the rank order of voice qualities were analyzed. For low-reverberation recordings, no systematic CPPS bias was introduced by dereverberation. In reverberant conditions, CPPS reductions were compensated after processing. For continuous speech, voice quality rankings were reconstructed, and CPPS values approached their anechoic reference levels across databases. These findings indicate that blind dereverberation can effectively mitigate room-acoustic distortions in objective voice quality assessment of continuous speech.
column7: Sven Franz(Jade University of Applied Sciences); Tanja Grewe(Jade University of Applied Sciences); Bernd T. Meyer(Carl von Ossietzky University); Jörg Bitzer(Jade University of Applied Sciences)
