column4: Queer inclusion in speech datasets: An audit and taxonomy of practical tensions
column6: In this paper, we examine speech datasets for their inclusion of LGBTQIA+, or queer, voices and provide a taxonomy of tensions to better understand why there is a lack of such voices in current speech technology datasets. Through an audit of six diverse speech datasets, we find that measurable queer representation is low (0–1.4% of speakers) - insufficient for robust disparity measurement. We take this community as a case study to consider what challenges and tensions are associated with collecting speech data from marginalized communities. For comparison, we audit an additional two datasets from the speech sciences that were created by, for, and with the queer community. We note that many customs in speech dataset collection efforts in AI and speech technology research may conflict with values emphasized in participatory approaches with marginalized communities, and provide a taxonomy describing these tensions.
column7: Brooklyn Sheppard(University of Calgary; Meta); Anaelia Ovalle(Meta); Adina Williams(Meta); Levent Sagun(Meta)

column4: Sexualised synthetic personas encode and amplify gendered power asymmetries through voice
column6: This work examines sexualised AI-generated English-speaking voices offered by a popular commercial platform. New technologies may enable sexual empowerment and greater diversity in gender expression, yet toxic masculinity, heteronormativity, and the abuse of women and LGBTQ+ people remain pervasive online. Drawing on a Feminist HCI perspective, we examine how commercial voice AI systems reproduce and circulate particular performances of gender. We conducted a listening experiment with a diverse group of listeners, combining quantitative adjective selection, qualitative free-text responses, and acoustic analysis. Participants evaluated male- and female-coded voices presented with either sexualised scripts or neutral text. Results reveal a narrow range of gender expression, largely binary and heteronormative. Female-coded voices are more frequently described using sexualised and submissive terms, while male-coded voices are more often associated with dominance and positive traits.
column7: Alice Ross(University of Edinburgh); Ariadna Sanchez(University of Edinburgh); Elin Kanhov(KTH Royal Institute of Technology); Catherine Lai(University of Edinburgh); Éva Székely(KTH Royal Institute of Technology)

column4: Lived Experiences of Power and Agency: Achieving Voice Sovereignty in Assistive Speech Technology for Nonbinary Users
column6: Speech-generating devices (SGDs) are essential tools for many speech-disabled individuals, yet current systems often reinforce normative assumptions about identity and communication. Prior research on gender expansive SGD users has largely focused on gendered voice options, with less attention to broader identity alignment and the technological conditions that shape users' agency. This study examines how gender expansive SGD users experience power over their voices using thematic analysis of qualitative survey data. Three themes emerged: (1) integration of SGDs into daily life, (2) identity expression, and (3) power and agency. Participants expressed the need for more responsive and reliable technology, inclusive and customizable voices, and greater autonomy in defining how their voices sound and are perceived. Ultimately, their perspectives call for a reimagining of SGD systems as tools for reclaiming the power of one's voice and the ability to define and enact one's will through it.
column7: Maxwell Hope(University of Delaware); Juliana Francis(KTH Royal Institute of Technology); Joakim Gustafson(KTH Royal Institute of Technology); Éva Székely(KTH Royal Institute of Technology)

column4: TMASC: Transmasculine Attitude and Speech Corpus
column6: We introduce the Transmasculine Attitudes and Speech Corpus (TMASC), a multimodal corpus of 196 transmasculine individuals, including questionnaire responses and 66 audio recordings. The questionnaire includes items exploring the vocal health of transmasculine individuals. The audio recordings include cough and throat-clearing samples, a reading passage, and additional session-specific questions. This paper outlines the development of this corpus and the data collection procedures. To illustrate the utility of this corpus, we present three case studies demonstrating how this crowd-sourced multimodal corpus can be used to support transmasculine individuals. These include the integration of perceptual and acoustic data, the identification of group-level characteristics, and the calibration of acoustic measurements.
column7: Sidney Wong(University of Otago; Te Pūnaha Matatini Centre of Research Excellence for Complex Systems)

column4: No-Shot Text-to-Speech: Limitations of Zero-Shot TTS and its Evaluation Methods in Representing Queer and Transgender Voices
column6: Gender expansive voices remain underrepresented in speech datasets, which could cause challenges with generalizability in zero-shot Text-To-Speech (TTS) systems. We evaluate six zero-shot TTS models on two datasets: one containing non gender expansive voices (N-GE) and one with gender expansive (GE) voices from self-identified speakers. Human ratings found that 2 of the 6 models synthesize less similar GE voices compared to N-GE voices, and 3 have improved performance for GE voices. Automated evaluations yield conflicting results, with speaker similarity and automated mean opinion score predictors rating performance of GE voices inconsistently between models and human ratings. This highlights a potential blind spot in evaluation pipelines, emphasizing a need for more representative data and metrics that better capture human perceptual judgments. Our findings stress the need to include transgender, queer, and minority communities in creation of better datasets and model training.
column7: Juliana Francis(KTH Royal Institute of Technology); Robin Netzorg(University of California, Berkeley); Joakim Gustafson(KTH Royal Institute of Technology); Éva Székely(KTH Royal Institute of Technology)

column4: The First Dravidian Speech Datasets for Transphobic and Homophobic Hate Speech: Creation, Annotation, and Multimodal Benchmarking
column6: Hate speech targeting the LGBTQIA+ community is under-explored in low-resource languages, particularly in speech. We address this gap by creating the first Dravidian speech datasets for homophobic and transphobic hate speech in Telugu and Malayalam, consisting of an Elicited Speech Dataset and a Social Media Audio Extract Dataset. These corpora fill a critical resource gap by capturing paralinguistic cues, which are essential for identifying hate speech from audio. We additionally provide a multimodal baseline that fuses Wav2Vec 2.0 acoustic embeddings and IndicBERT linguistic embeddings using attention-based fusion, and evaluate robustness across matched, cross-domain, and hybrid conditions. Results show strong performance in-domain but degradation under domain shift, highlighting challenges in acoustic transfer. Our primary contribution is the development and analysis of the first Dravidian LGBTQIA+ speech hate-speech datasets, enabling future research on speech-based detection.
column7: K N Lakshmi(Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham); K HEMAVARDHAN REDDY(Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham); A VENKATA SATYA(Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham); Kota Venkata VAMSHIDHAR REDDY(Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham); JYOTHISH LAL G(Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham); Premjith B(Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham); Jesin James(University of Auckland)

column4: Masculinity and Sexual Orientation as Predictors of f0 Variation in the Speech of Australian English Speaking Men
column6: The effect of sexual orientation (SO) on the fundamental frequency of men's voices has been widely studied since the late twentieth century. Less widely studied has been the effect on fundamental frequency of men's orientations towards traditional masculinity, and no study has yet investigated the impact of either of these variables in the Australian English (AusE) context. Presented here are the results of an examination of the effect of SO and orientation toward masculinity on three f0-derived variables, using speech data elicited from 77 male speakers of AusE. Referential topic (LGBTQ vs neutral) was also investigated. Results demonstrated that none of these independent variables significantly impacted local f0, but that SO, orientation toward masculinity and topic all affected f0 dynamicity, and SO and topic both affected f0 range. In all cases, however, these effects occurred in complex interactions with each other and with speaker age.
column7: Timothy Shea(Macquarie University); Hannah White(LMU Munich); Joshua Penney(Macquarie University); Anita Szakay(Macquarie University); Felicity Cox(Macquarie University)

column4: Towards participatory speech dataset curation: A queer case study and conceptual framework
column6: In this paper, we motivate the need for a participatory speech dataset creation framework through a case study of the LGBTQIA+, or queer, community - a community with documented concerns about AI and reported harms, including attempts to develop 'gaydar' technologies that purportedly identify individuals as queer. We review common speech data collection practices, why these methods may be unsuitable for engaging with queer speakers, and discuss previous efforts in participatory AI with queer community engagement, as well as participatory endeavours specific to speech data collection for other marginalized communities. From this review, we develop a conceptual framework for participatory speech data curation by, for, and with marginalized communities drawing on insights from co-design and knowledge sharing. We propose a framework comprising overlapping and two-way processes of defining a community, project formulation, modes of participation, and personal autonomy.
column7: Brooklyn Sheppard(University of Calgary; Meta); Anaelia Ovalle(Meta); Adina Williams(Meta); Levent Sagun(Meta)
